title: Why the Moon seems to change shape, and how eclipses happen
playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if done at home today. Changes made: the ball and lamp test now says to use one bare bulb or a phone torch in a fully dark room, because soft room light blurs the line between light and dark. It tells the child to hold the ball a little above their head, because otherwise the head's shadow darkens the full Moon. That accidental eclipse is now its own step. The shadow test uses a small torch 2 metres away, because a big lamp gives fuzzy shadows, and a lime about a quarter as wide as a football, the real size ratio. The Moon diary now looks every second evening for about two weeks, not every night for a month, because after Purnima the Moon rises too late for a child's bedtime. The last look is in the morning instead. It says cloudy nights are normal, so start outside the monsoon if you can. The rising Moon test uses a masoor dal at arm's length, which just covers the Moon, and says to look the night after Purnima if buildings hide the horizon. Both games were played through: Moon Pairs works alone against the clock, and Eclipse Hunters was changed so a tilt card is turned every time a Moon passes new or full Moon, not only on an exact landing. Before, a player could go 15 laps without an eclipse. Now a player catches about 2 eclipses in 5 laps, which fits a 20-minute game and gives a solo player a score to beat. The sky activities now work from a city window or balcony: west-facing early in the month, east-facing near Purnima. A parent should know that they need a clear sky, and that a calendar marking Amavasya and Purnima makes planning much easier.

summary.text: The Moon makes no light of its own, but the Sun always lights half of it. As the Moon goes round the Earth each month, we see more or less of that lit half, so its shape seems to change. The Moon spins once for each trip round us, so we always see the same face. When the Sun, the Earth and the Moon line up exactly, a shadow falls and we get an eclipse. Indian calendars count the Moon's days, called tithis, and many festivals still follow them.
summary.art: A girl at a balcony railing at dusk holding a moon diary open, with a row of drawn Moon shapes from thin crescent to full, and the real crescent Moon low in the sky above the buildings.

intro.hook: The Moon is a round ball of rock. So why does it look like a thin curve on some nights, and a full circle on others?
intro.text: People everywhere have watched the Moon grow from a thin curve to a full circle and back again, about once a month. Farmers and fishing families planned their work by it, and Indian calendars still count its days. The word 'month' even comes from the word 'Moon'. But the Moon makes no light, and it never changes its size. So what changes? In this unit you will make every Moon shape yourself, with a ball and a lamp in a dark room, and find out.
intro.art: A row of Moon shapes from thin crescent to full, above a fisherwoman on a boat, a farmer in a field and a child at a city window, all looking up.

outcomes: I can show with a ball and a lamp why the Moon seems to change shape, and name its phases in order.
I can keep a Moon diary: I draw the Moon's shape, the date, the time and where it is, and I spot the pattern.
I can explain why we always see the same face of the Moon: it spins once for each trip round the Earth, because the Earth's pull slowed it down.
I can explain solar and lunar eclipses using shadows, and say why they do not happen every month.
I can say how Indian calendars count the Moon's days, the tithis and the pakshas, and name festivals set by the Moon.
I can tell the main idea of how the Moon was made, and what scientists still argue about.
I can say what Aryabhata, Wang Zhenyi and others found about the Moon, and give examples of living things that keep time by it.

terms.meaning: The shape of the lit part of the Moon that we see on a night. The Moon goes through all its phases once a month.
terms.example: A thin crescent, a half Moon and a full Moon are three phases.
terms.art: Eight small Moon shapes in a row, from a thin crescent to full and back.

terms.meaning: The night when we cannot see the Moon. Its lit half faces away from us, towards the Sun.
terms.example: Diwali falls on an Amavasya, so the sky is dark and the lamps shine bright.
terms.art: A dark night sky over rooftops lit with rows of diyas, and no Moon.

terms.meaning: The night when we see the whole lit half of the Moon, a full round circle.
terms.example: Guru Purnima and Buddha Purnima fall on full Moon nights.
terms.art: A big round full Moon rising over a lake, with its reflection on the water.

terms.meaning: A thin curved Moon, shaped like a fingernail clipping.
terms.example: Two or three days after Amavasya, a thin crescent Moon shows low in the west just after sunset.
terms.art: A thin crescent Moon lying on its back like a boat, above a sunset.

terms.meaning: A Moon that looks like half a circle. It is called a quarter Moon because it comes a quarter of the way through the month.
terms.example: About a week after Amavasya you see a half Moon high in the sky at sunset.
terms.art: A half Moon, lit on the right, in an evening sky.

terms.meaning: A Moon that is more than half lit but not yet full. It looks like a slightly squashed circle.
terms.example: Two or three nights before Purnima, the Moon is gibbous.
terms.art: A fat gibbous Moon, one edge a little flattened.

terms.meaning: Growing. Each night, we see a little more of the Moon's lit half.
terms.example: From Amavasya to Purnima the Moon is waxing. This is the bright half of the month, Shukla Paksha.
terms.art: Five Moon shapes getting bigger from left to right, with a small arrow.

terms.meaning: Shrinking. Each night, we see a little less of the Moon's lit half.
terms.example: From Purnima to Amavasya the Moon is waning. This is the dark half of the month, Krishna Paksha.
terms.art: Five Moon shapes getting smaller from left to right.

terms.meaning: The time from one new Moon to the next. It is about 29 and a half days.
terms.example: From one Diwali Amavasya to the next Amavasya is one lunar month.
terms.art: A circle of 29 small Moon pictures, like a necklace.

terms.meaning: A Moon day in the Indian calendar. There are 30 tithis in each lunar month. A tithi is usually close to one day long, but it can be a few hours shorter or longer.
terms.example: Ganesh Chaturthi falls on the fourth tithi, chaturthi, of the bright half of the month.
terms.art: A wall calendar page with small Moon shapes printed on some of the dates.

terms.meaning: Half of a lunar month, about 15 tithis. Shukla Paksha is the bright half, when the Moon grows. Krishna Paksha is the dark half, when it shrinks.
terms.example: Navratri begins in Shukla Paksha, as the Moon starts to grow.
terms.art: A circle split into a bright half with growing Moons and a dark half with shrinking Moons.

terms.meaning: The path one thing takes as it goes round another.
terms.example: The Moon's orbit takes it all the way round the Earth.
terms.art: The Earth with a dotted circle around it and the Moon on the circle.

terms.meaning: When a moon spins exactly once for each trip round its planet, so it always shows the planet the same face. The planet's pull slowed its spin until it fell into step.
terms.example: Our Moon is tidally locked to the Earth. So are the four big moons of Jupiter.
terms.art: The Moon going round the Earth in four positions, with a small flag on the Moon always pointing at the Earth.

terms.meaning: The half of the Moon that always faces away from the Earth. We never see it from here. It gets just as much sunlight as the side we see.
terms.example: A Chinese spacecraft, Chang'e 4, was the first to land on the far side, in 2019.
terms.art: The Moon split down the middle: one side with big dark patches, the other side pale and covered in craters.

terms.meaning: Sunlight that bounces off the Earth, lands on the dark part of the Moon, and bounces back to us. It makes the dark part of a crescent Moon glow faintly.
terms.example: Look at a thin crescent Moon just after sunset. You can often see the whole round Moon, faintly grey.
terms.art: A bright thin crescent with the rest of the Moon's circle glowing faint grey.

terms.meaning: When one thing in space moves into another's shadow, or blocks its light from us.
terms.example: In a lunar eclipse, the Moon moves into the Earth's shadow.
terms.art: A lamp, a ball and a smaller ball in a line, with a shadow falling from one onto the other.

terms.meaning: When the Moon passes between the Sun and the Earth, and blocks the Sun. It can only happen at new Moon.
terms.example: On 22 July 2009, just after sunrise, the Sun went completely dark for a few minutes over Varanasi and Patna.
terms.art: A dark Moon covering the Sun, with a glowing white ring of light around it.

terms.meaning: When the Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon, and the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. It can only happen at full Moon.
terms.example: In a total lunar eclipse the Moon often turns a coppery red.
terms.art: A full Moon slowly being covered by a curved shadow edge, the covered part glowing red.

terms.meaning: A dark area where light cannot reach, because something is in the way.
terms.example: Your own shadow on the ground at noon. The Earth's shadow stretches far out into space.
terms.art: A child's shadow on the ground, and the Earth with a long cone of shadow behind it.

terms.meaning: In Indian astronomy, the names of the two points where the Moon's path crosses the Sun's path in the sky. Eclipses can only happen when the Moon is near one of them.
terms.example: Old stories said Rahu swallowed the Sun. Astronomers like Aryabhata kept the names, but used them for these two crossing points.
terms.art: Two tilted rings crossing each other at two points, one marked Rahu and one marked Ketu.

terms.meaning: The main idea of how the Moon was made. A planet about the size of Mars crashed into the young Earth, and the Moon formed from the hot rock thrown out.
terms.example: Scientists sometimes call the crashing planet Theia.
terms.art: A small glowing planet striking the young Earth, and a ring of hot rock spreading out.

terms.meaning: An extra month that Indian calendars add about once every three years. It keeps the Moon months in step with the seasons.
terms.example: Without adhik maas, Diwali would slowly drift from autumn into summer.
terms.art: A calendar with an extra page slipped in, labelled with a small extra Moon.

terms.meaning: The rising Moon looks much bigger near the horizon than when it is high in the sky. It is really the same size. The difference is made by our brains.
terms.example: A full Moon rising behind a water tank looks huge. Three hours later, high up, it looks small.
terms.art: A huge orange Moon rising behind a water tank, and the same Moon small and white high above.

explanations.concept: Half of the Moon is always lit
explanations.definition: The Moon makes no light of its own. The Sun always lights exactly half of it, the half facing the Sun. The other half is in the Moon's own shadow.
explanations.description: You may already know that moonlight is sunlight bouncing off the Moon. Here is what follows from that. At every moment, one half of the Moon is in daylight and one half is in night, just like the Earth. The Moon never grows or shrinks. What changes is how much of its daylight half is turned towards us. When the lit half faces us, we see a full Moon. When it faces away, we see nothing. In between, we see a slice of it.
examples: Hold an orange near a lamp in a dark room. One half is always bright. Walk round it, and the bright part you see changes shape.
The Earth has phases too, seen from the Moon. Astronauts going round the Moon photographed a half-lit Earth rising over its edge.
explanations.art: The Moon in space with the Sun far to the left: its left half bright, its right half dark, and a child's eye on Earth seeing only part of the bright half.
explanations.context: This card explains the one idea behind all the Moon's shapes: the Sun always lights half of it.

explanations.concept: The phases in order, and why the month is 29 and a half days
explanations.definition: The Moon's phases always come in the same order: new, crescent, half, gibbous, full, gibbous, half, crescent, and new again. One full round takes about 29 and a half days.
explanations.description: The Moon goes round the Earth. When it is between us and the Sun, its lit half faces away, and we see a new Moon. A quarter of the way round, we see half of the lit half: a half Moon. Halfway round, on the far side of us from the Sun, we see all of the lit half: a full Moon. Then the shapes shrink again in the opposite order. In India, a growing Moon is lit on its right side, the side towards the setting Sun. A shrinking Moon is lit on its left. Here is a surprise. The Moon goes once round the Earth, measured against the stars, in about 27 and a third days. But a new Moon to the next new Moon takes about 29 and a half. While the Moon goes round, the Earth also moves along its own path round the Sun. So the Moon needs about two more days to catch up and line up with the Sun again.
examples: From one Amavasya to the next is about 29 and a half days. So calendars give lunar months 29 or 30 days.
The bright curved edge of the Moon always points towards the Sun. In the evening, that is the place where the Sun has just set.
explanations.art: A circle of eight Moon positions around the Earth, each with a small picture of how that Moon looks from Earth, and the Sun's rays coming from the left.
explanations.context: This card puts the Moon's shapes in order, and explains why one full round takes about 29 and a half days.

explanations.concept: Each phase rises at its own time
explanations.definition: The Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day, on average. So each phase is up at a different time of day and night.
explanations.description: The Moon moves a little further round the Earth every day. So the spinning Earth needs a little extra time to turn us back to face it. That extra time is about 50 minutes, though it varies. A new Moon rises and sets with the Sun, hidden in its glare. A growing half Moon rises around noon and is high in the sky at sunset. A full Moon rises as the Sun sets and is up all night. A shrinking half Moon rises around midnight and is still up in the morning. So the Moon is not only a night thing. For about half of each month you can see it in the daytime, if you know where to look.
examples: On Purnima, look east at sunset. The full Moon rises as the Sun goes down in the west.
A few days after Purnima, look west in the morning on the way to school. The Moon is often still there, pale against the blue sky.
explanations.art: A clock face with four small Moons placed at the times they rise: new Moon at 6 in the morning, half Moon at noon, full Moon at 6 in the evening, the other half Moon at midnight.
explanations.context: People often think the Moon only comes out at night. This card shows when each Moon shape rises.

explanations.concept: Why we always see the same face: tidal locking
explanations.definition: The Moon spins once on its own axis for every trip it makes round the Earth. So the same side always faces us. This is called tidal locking.
explanations.description: Many people think the Moon does not spin at all. It does, very slowly, once every 27 and a third days. That is exactly the time it takes to go round us once. So it keeps its face towards us, just as you do when you walk round a chair while always facing it. It was not always like this. Long ago, the young Moon spun faster. The Earth's gravity pulled on the Moon's rock and stretched it into a very slight bulge, pointing at the Earth. As the Moon spun, the bulge was carried away, and the Earth's pull kept tugging it back. That tug worked like a brake. Over millions of years it slowed the Moon's spin until the bulge stayed pointing at the Earth. Then the spin and the trip matched, and they have stayed matched ever since. The Moon does the same to the Earth. Its pull on our oceans and rocks is slowly slowing the Earth's spin too. One day, very far in the future, the Earth might always show the Moon one face. That would take so long that the Sun will change first.
examples: Walk round a chair while always looking at it. When you get back to the start, you have faced every wall of the room once. You turned round once, just like the Moon.
Most big moons in the solar system are tidally locked, like Jupiter's moons Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto.
Pluto and its moon Charon are locked to each other. Each always shows the other the same face.
explanations.art: The Moon going round the Earth in four positions, drawn with a slightly stretched egg shape, its long end always pointing at the Earth.
explanations.context: Why do we only ever see one side of the Moon? This card explains how the Earth's pull slowed the Moon's spin until it fell into step.

explanations.concept: The far side is not dark, and the Moon has two different faces
explanations.description: People sometimes call the far side of the Moon 'the dark side'. That is wrong. It gets just as much sunlight as the side we see. On the night of Amavasya, when we see no Moon, the far side is in full daylight. Nobody saw it until 1959, when a Soviet spacecraft, Luna 3, flew round and photographed it. Scientists got a surprise. Our side has big dark patches, called seas. They are not water. They are huge plains of old, dark lava that flooded out long ago. The far side has almost none. Its crust is also thicker. In 2019, China's Chang'e 4 became the first spacecraft to land on the far side. In 2024, Chang'e 6 brought rock from the far side back to Earth for the first time. Why the two faces are so different is still argued about.
examples: The dark patches on our side make the 'face' or the 'hare' that people see in the Moon.
A rover on the far side cannot talk to Earth directly, because the whole Moon is in the way. China put a relay satellite, Queqiao, beyond the Moon to pass messages along.

perspectives.explanation: The side facing the young Earth stayed hotter, because the newborn Earth was glowing hot nearby. So the crust on that side stayed thin, and lava could break through it easily. On the cooler far side, the crust grew thicker.

A second, smaller moon may once have crashed gently into the far side, piling up the thick crust there. Others think a giant impact on the far side shook the whole Moon. Nobody knows yet which idea is right.

explanations.art: The two faces of the Moon side by side: the near side with its dark lava seas, the far side pale and full of craters, a small lander with a rover on it.
explanations.context: We only ever see one side of the Moon. This card is about the other side, and why it looks so different.

explanations.concept: Earthshine: the Earth lights up the Moon's night
explanations.definition: Earthshine is sunlight that bounces off the Earth onto the dark part of the Moon, and back to our eyes. It makes the dark part of a thin crescent glow faintly.
explanations.description: Look at a thin crescent Moon two or three evenings after Amavasya. Very often you can see the rest of the Moon's circle too, glowing a soft grey. That faint light has made a long trip. It left the Sun, bounced off the Earth's clouds, seas and land, travelled to the Moon, bounced again and came back to you. Leonardo da Vinci worked this out about 500 years ago and wrote it in his notebooks. When we see a thin crescent Moon, someone standing on the Moon would see a nearly full Earth, shining big and bright. The Earth reflects sunlight much better than the Moon does, because of its white clouds.
examples: Earthshine is easiest to see on a crescent in the evening sky, or a crescent in the early morning before Amavasya.
Scientists measure earthshine to find out how much sunlight the whole Earth bounces back, which helps them study its clouds.
explanations.art: A thin bright crescent Moon with the rest of its circle faintly glowing, and a dotted line showing sunlight bouncing from the Sun to the Earth to the Moon and back.
explanations.context: Sometimes you can see the whole Moon even when only a thin crescent is lit. This card explains the faint glow.

explanations.concept: How was the Moon made? The detective story
explanations.description: Most scientists think the Moon was born in a giant crash, about four and a half billion years ago. A young planet about the size of Mars, which they call Theia, hit the young Earth. Hot rock was flung into space and gathered into the Moon. How do we know anything at all about something nobody saw? Like detectives, scientists use clues. The rocks that astronauts brought back are almost exactly like the rock of the Earth's outer layers. The Moon has only a tiny iron centre, while the Earth has a big one. A crash that splashed out the Earth's outer rock would explain both. Computers let scientists run the crash again and again with different sizes and speeds. In 2001, Robin Canup and Erik Asphaug showed that a glancing blow from a Mars-sized planet could make a Moon like ours. But there is a puzzle. In many of these computer crashes, the Moon ends up made mostly of Theia. Then why are its rocks such a close match to the Earth's?
examples: Astronauts brought back about 382 kilograms of Moon rock between 1969 and 1972.
Tiny crystals in a Moon rock show the Moon was already solid about 4.46 billion years ago.

perspectives.who: Most scientists, following William Hartmann and Donald Davis (1975), and Robin Canup (2001)
perspectives.explanation: One giant glancing crash with a Mars-sized planet threw out rock that slowly gathered into the Moon.
Their more detailed computer crashes suggest the Moon may have formed in just a few hours, flung out in one piece, not slowly gathered over years.

perspectives.who: Raluca Rufu, Oded Aharonson and Hagai Perets (2017)
perspectives.explanation: Maybe there was no single giant crash. Many smaller crashes each made a small moon, and the small moons joined into one.
Two huge blobs of unusual rock deep inside the Earth, near its core, might be the leftovers of Theia. This is an idea, still being tested.

explanations.art: Detective style: a girl scientist with a magnifying glass looking at a Moon rock and an Earth rock side by side, a computer screen behind her showing two planets colliding.
explanations.context: Nobody saw the Moon being born. This card is about the clues scientists use to work out how it happened, and the ideas they still argue about.

explanations.definition: An eclipse happens when the Sun, the Earth and the Moon line up. In a solar eclipse, the Moon blocks the Sun from part of the Earth. In a lunar eclipse, the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.
explanations.description: Everything lit by the Sun throws a shadow behind it, far out into space. Usually the Moon's shadow and the Earth's shadow fall on nothing. A solar eclipse can only happen at new Moon, when the Moon is between us and the Sun. The Moon is small, so its dark shadow only touches a small patch of the Earth. Only people in that patch see the Sun fully covered. A lunar eclipse can only happen at full Moon, when the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon. The Earth's shadow is much bigger than the Moon, so it can swallow the whole Moon. Everyone on the night side of the Earth can see it. During a total lunar eclipse the Moon turns coppery red. A little sunlight bends through the Earth's air and reaches it. The air lets the red light through and scatters the blue away, the same way it makes sunsets red. So the red Moon is lit by all the sunrises and sunsets on Earth at that moment.
examples: On the night of 7 September 2025, people all over India watched a total lunar eclipse turn the Moon red.
A solar eclipse is the only kind that is dangerous to watch, because people may look at the Sun. Never look at the Sun directly, eclipse or not. A lunar eclipse is safe to watch with bare eyes.
explanations.art: Two panels: the Moon between the Sun and the Earth with a tiny shadow spot on the Earth, then the Earth between the Sun and a red Moon sitting inside the Earth's long shadow.
explanations.context: This card explains what an eclipse really is: the Sun, the Earth and the Moon lining up, so a shadow falls on one of them.

explanations.concept: Why there is not an eclipse every month: Rahu and Ketu
explanations.definition: The Moon's path round the Earth is tilted a little, about 5 degrees, compared with the Earth's path round the Sun. So at most new and full Moons, the shadows miss. Eclipses only happen when a new or full Moon falls close to one of the two crossing points of the paths.
explanations.description: If the paths were flat, there would be a solar eclipse every Amavasya and a lunar eclipse every Purnima. But the Moon usually passes a little above or a little below the line between the Sun and the Earth. Its path crosses the Sun's path in the sky at only two points. Indian astronomers named these two points Rahu and Ketu. Long ago, a story said a demon called Rahu swallowed the Sun or the Moon. The astronomers kept the old names but used them for something they could calculate. An eclipse can only happen when the new or full Moon is near Rahu or Ketu. That happens roughly every six months. So eclipses come in 'seasons', about half a year apart.
examples: Every year has at least two solar eclipses somewhere on the Earth. Many of them are only partial, with part of the Sun left showing.
About 2,500 years ago, astronomers in Babylon noticed that eclipses repeat in a pattern every 18 years and 11 days. They used it to predict them.
explanations.art: A hula hoop tilted inside another hoop, the two crossing at two points labelled Rahu and Ketu, with a small Moon passing above the line.
explanations.context: If eclipses come from lining up, why don't we get one every full Moon? This card explains the tilt, and where the names Rahu and Ketu come from.

explanations.definition: Aryabhata, an Indian astronomer, wrote in 499 CE that the Moon is lit by the Sun, and that eclipses are caused by shadows, not by a demon.
explanations.description: Aryabhata lived in Kusumapura, near today's Patna. In his book, the Aryabhatiya, in the part called the Golapada, he wrote two things clearly. Half of the Earth, of each planet and of the Moon is dark from its own shadow, and the half facing the Sun is bright. And in a solar eclipse the Moon covers the Sun, while in a lunar eclipse the great shadow of the Earth covers the Moon. He also gave ways to calculate when eclipses would happen. Later Indian astronomers, like Varahamihira and Lalla, agreed that eclipses are shadows. The great mathematician Brahmagupta argued against Aryabhata on several points. Much later, about the year 1030, a Persian scholar called Al-Biruni studied Indian astronomy. He thought Brahmagupta knew the shadow explanation was right, and spoke up for the old Rahu story to keep peace with religious tradition.
examples: Anaxagoras in Greece, about 2,450 years ago, also said the Moon shines by the Sun's light and that eclipses are shadows.
Aristotle noticed that the Earth's shadow on the Moon during a lunar eclipse always has a curved edge. Only a round ball always throws a round shadow, so the Earth must be round.
explanations.art: Aryabhata writing on palm-leaf pages by lamplight, with a drawing beside him of the Sun, the Earth's shadow and a darkened Moon.
explanations.context: About 1,500 years ago, an Indian astronomer explained eclipses with shadows. This card is about what he wrote, and who argued with him.

explanations.definition: Wang Zhenyi, a young Chinese astronomer who lived from 1768 to 1797, explained lunar eclipses with a model made from a lamp, a round table and a mirror.
explanations.description: In Wang Zhenyi's time in China, girls were not supposed to study. Her grandfather had a big library, and she read his books on astronomy. She taught herself mathematics. Many people then believed a heavenly dog ate the Moon during an eclipse, and they banged drums and gongs to scare it away. Wang Zhenyi wanted to show what really happened. In a garden pavilion, she hung a lamp from the roof as the Sun. A round table was the Earth. A round mirror was the Moon. She moved them until the table's shadow fell on the mirror, just as the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. She wrote about it in an essay explaining the lunar eclipse. She wrote about a dozen books on astronomy and mathematics before she died, aged only 29. She also wrote poems arguing that daughters can be as heroic as sons.
examples: You can make her model at home with a lamp, a big ball and a small ball.
A crater on the planet Venus is named after Wang Zhenyi.
explanations.art: A young woman in a Chinese garden pavilion at night, a lamp hanging from the roof, adjusting a round mirror so that the shadow of a round table falls on it.
explanations.context: About 240 years ago, a young woman in China built a model of an eclipse from things in her house. This card is her story.

explanations.definition: Eclipses let scientists study things the Sun's glare usually hides. A new element, helium, was found in an eclipse seen from India in 1868. An eclipse in 1919 helped test Einstein's idea that gravity bends light.
explanations.description: On 18 August 1868, a French astronomer, Jules Janssen, watched a total solar eclipse from Guntur, in today's Andhra Pradesh. He split the light from the Sun's glowing edge into its colours. He saw a bright yellow line that matched no known substance. An English astronomer, Norman Lockyer, said it came from a new element. He named it helium, after Helios, the Greek word for the Sun. Helium was found on the Sun before anyone found it on Earth. In 1919, astronomers led by Arthur Eddington photographed stars near the Sun during an eclipse. The stars seemed slightly shifted from their usual places. That fitted Einstein's idea that the Sun's gravity bends the paths of light passing near it. In Einstein's idea, gravity bends space and time, and light follows those bends.
examples: Helium is the gas in party balloons that float. Its name comes from the Sun, where it was first found.
Light from far galaxies is bent by gravity too. Scientists call this gravitational lensing.
explanations.art: An astronomer at a telescope in Guntur in 1868, under a darkened Sun with a glowing ring, a strip of rainbow colours with one bright yellow line in front of him.
explanations.context: Eclipses are not only beautiful. This card is about two big discoveries made during eclipses, one of them from India.

explanations.definition: Indian calendars count months by the Moon. Each lunar month has 30 tithis, split into a bright half, Shukla Paksha, and a dark half, Krishna Paksha. An extra month is added about once every three years to keep in step with the seasons.
explanations.description: A tithi is the time the Moon takes to move a set step further from the Sun in the sky. Because the Moon's speed changes, a tithi can be a few hours shorter or longer than a day. In much of North India, a month ends on Purnima. In much of South and West India, a month ends on Amavasya. Twelve Moon months make about 354 days. That is 11 days short of a Sun year of 365 days. So every three years or so, an extra month, the adhik maas, is slipped in. That keeps Diwali in autumn and Holi in spring. The Islamic calendar is a pure Moon calendar with no extra month. So Eid and Ramzan come about 11 days earlier each year, and slowly move through every season. Chinese, Jewish and Buddhist calendars also follow the Moon. Easter falls on the Sunday after the first full Moon of spring.
examples: Diwali falls on Amavasya. Holi, Raksha Bandhan, Guru Purnima, Buddha Purnima and Sharad Purnima fall on full Moons. Karva Chauth ends when the Moon rises. Eid begins when the new crescent is seen.
Sun festivals stay on nearly the same date each year. Makar Sankranti and Pongal fall around 14 January.
explanations.art: A wall calendar with small Moon shapes printed on some dates, diyas on the Amavasya square, coloured powder on the Holi Purnima square and a thin crescent on the Eid square.
explanations.context: Why does Diwali fall on a different date each year? This card explains how Indian calendars count by the Moon.

explanations.concept: Living things that keep Moon time
explanations.description: Many living things keep time by the Moon, for their own reasons, not ours. On the Great Barrier Reef in Australia, many corals release their eggs together on a few nights after a full Moon in late spring. Each coral polyp seems to sense the moonlight. Dung beetles in Africa can roll their dung balls in a straight line on moonlit nights. They steer by the way moonlight is spread across the sky. Lions hunt most successfully on dark nights, so the people who live near them are in most danger in the days after the full Moon. Do people keep Moon time too? That is argued about.
examples: Spring tides, the highest high tides, come at new Moon and full Moon. Many sea creatures time their egg-laying to the tides.
Night animals like owls, bats and mice change how they behave on bright full-Moon nights.

perspectives.who: Leandro Casiraghi, Horacio de la Iglesia and their team (2021)
perspectives.explanation: People in villages without electricity in Argentina, and students in the city of Seattle, went to sleep later and slept less on the nights before a full Moon.
Other studies found little or no link between the Moon and human sleep. The question is still open.

explanations.art: A full Moon over a coral reef with clouds of tiny pink eggs rising, a dung beetle rolling a ball under the Moon, and an owl on a branch.
explanations.context: People are not the only ones who watch the Moon. This card is about animals that keep time by it, and whether we do too.

explanations.concept: The Earth and the Moon go round each other
explanations.definition: The Moon does not simply go round a still Earth. The Earth and the Moon both go round a shared point between them. Because the Earth is so much heavier, that point lies inside the Earth, about 4,700 kilometres from its centre.
explanations.description: Think of a heavy grown-up and a small child holding hands and spinning round. The child swings in a big circle. The grown-up wobbles in a small circle. Both turn round a point between them, close to the grown-up. The Earth and the Moon are like that. Each month, the Earth wobbles in a small circle as the Moon swings round. They also change each other in other ways. The Earth's pull locked the Moon's face. The Moon's pull makes our tides, and slowly slows the Earth's spin. As it does, the Moon drifts about 3.8 centimetres further away every year. Scientists measure this by bouncing laser light off mirrors left on the Moon by astronauts.
examples: Astronomers find planets round other stars partly this way. A planet makes its star wobble a little, just as the Moon makes the Earth wobble.
Some scientists think the Moon helps keep the Earth's tilt steady, and so keeps our seasons steady. Others think the Earth would manage without it.
explanations.art: A grown-up and a child holding hands and spinning, beside a drawing of the Earth and the Moon both circling a small dot just inside the Earth.
explanations.context: We say the Moon goes round the Earth. This card shows that the Earth and the Moon both move, round a point they share.

explanations.concept: The perfect eclipse will not last for ever
explanations.definition: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon, and also about 400 times further away. So they look the same size in our sky, and the Moon can just cover the Sun. Because the Moon is drifting away, this will not always be true.
explanations.description: In a total solar eclipse, the Moon covers the Sun almost exactly. That lets people see the Sun's faint outer glow, the corona, which is usually hidden by glare. This perfect fit is a coincidence of our time. The Moon moves about 3.8 centimetres further away every year. Long ago, it was closer and looked bigger, so it covered the Sun with room to spare. In several hundred million years, it will look too small to cover the Sun completely. Then there will be no more total solar eclipses on Earth, only ones where a ring of Sun is left showing.
examples: When the Moon is a little further away than usual, it cannot cover the whole Sun. A ring of Sun shows round it. This is called an annular eclipse. South India saw one on 26 December 2019.
Hold a coin at arm's length. Move it until it just covers a far-away lamp. Further away it is too small, nearer it is too big.
explanations.art: Three solar eclipses in a row: long ago a big Moon covering the Sun with room to spare, today an exact fit with the glowing corona, far future a small Moon with a ring of Sun showing.
explanations.context: This card is about a lucky coincidence that gives us total solar eclipses, and why it will not last.

agreed.text: The Moon makes no light. Half of it is always lit by the Sun, and its phases are how much of that lit half we see.
agreed.evidence: A ball and a lamp make every phase in the right order. The lit side of the Moon always points towards the Sun in the sky. Astronauts and spacecraft near the Moon have photographed the Earth half lit, so the Earth has phases too.

agreed.text: The Moon spins once for each trip round the Earth, so we always see the same face.
agreed.evidence: Every photograph of the Moon from Earth, for as long as there have been cameras, shows the same seas and craters. Spacecraft have mapped the far side, which looks different.

agreed.text: Solar eclipses happen only at new Moon, and lunar eclipses only at full Moon, when the Sun, the Earth and the Moon line up.
agreed.evidence: Astronomers predict eclipses to the minute, hundreds of years ahead. They use these rules, the tilt of the Moon's path and careful measurements of how the Moon and the Earth move.

agreed.text: The Moon is slowly moving away from the Earth, and the Earth's spin is slowly slowing down.
agreed.evidence: Laser light bounced off mirrors left on the Moon by astronauts shows it moves about 3.8 centimetres further away each year. Ancient records of eclipses, from Babylon and China, also show the Earth's spin has slowed.

agreed.text: The Moon is about four and a half billion years old, and was probably made in a giant crash.
agreed.evidence: Moon rocks have been dated in laboratories. They are made of rock very like the Earth's outer layers, and the Moon has only a tiny iron centre. Exactly how the crash happened is still argued about.

challenging.claim: The Moon changes shape because the Earth's shadow covers part of it.
challenging.who: Many children and grown-ups. It is one of the most common ideas about the Moon.
challenging.for: Shadows make things dark, and the Earth does throw a shadow into space.
challenging.against: The Earth's shadow points away from the Sun. So it could only fall on the Moon when the Moon is opposite the Sun, and that is exactly when we see a full Moon. A crescent shows when the Moon is near the Sun in the sky, where the Earth's shadow can never reach. The Earth's shadow touches the Moon only in a lunar eclipse. The ball and lamp test makes every phase without any shadow falling on the ball.
challenging.context: Why does the Moon look like a crescent or a half? This card is about a very common wrong answer.

challenging.claim: The far side of the Moon is always dark.
challenging.who: Many people. Even some songs and films call it 'the dark side of the Moon'.
challenging.for: We never see the far side, so it seems hidden in darkness.
challenging.against: The far side gets just as much sunlight as the near side. It is lit when our side is dark. On Amavasya, the far side is in full daylight. 'Far side' is the right name, not 'dark side'.
challenging.context: This card is about the half of the Moon we never see, and whether it is really dark.

challenging.claim: The Moon does not spin at all.
challenging.who: Many people, because the Moon always shows us the same face.
challenging.for: From the Earth, the Moon's face never seems to turn.
challenging.against: Walk round a chair while always looking at it. By the end you have faced every wall of the room. You turned once. The Moon does the same. Measured against the stars, it spins once every 27 and a third days.
challenging.context: The Moon always shows us one face. This card asks whether that means it does not spin.

challenging.claim: Eclipses are dangerous for food, water and people, so everyone must stay inside.
challenging.who: Old customs in many places, including parts of India. Some families still fast, or throw away cooked food, during an eclipse.
challenging.for: Eclipses are rare and strange, and people long ago did not know what caused them. Customs often hold a family's memories and feelings, and many people value them for that.
challenging.against: An eclipse is a shadow. It sends nothing harmful down onto food, water or people. The one real danger is looking straight at the Sun during a solar eclipse, which can burn the eyes. Scientists and families all over the world watch eclipses safely, with eclipse glasses for the Sun and bare eyes for the Moon.
challenging.context: Many families have customs during an eclipse. This card asks what science says about the danger.

challenging.claim: The full Moon makes people and animals behave strangely.
challenging.who: A very old belief. The English word 'lunatic' comes from 'luna', the Latin word for the Moon.
challenging.for: Many nurses and police officers say full-Moon nights feel busier. Some animals really do change what they do when the Moon is bright.
challenging.against: Large studies of hospitals, police records and births have found no real link between the full Moon and strange behaviour in people. We remember the busy full-Moon nights and forget the busy other nights. Some newer studies suggest people sleep a little less before a full Moon, but others found no effect.
challenging.context: People have long said the full Moon makes us act oddly. This card weighs the evidence.

challenging.claim: Brahmagupta argued against Aryabhata's shadow explanation of eclipses only to please religious leaders.
challenging.who: Al-Biruni, a Persian scholar who studied Indian astronomy, about the year 1030
challenging.for: Brahmagupta was a brilliant mathematician. He calculated eclipses using shadows himself, so he must have known the shadow explanation worked.
challenging.against: We cannot know what Brahmagupta really thought. He may have honestly believed both could be true at once, or had other reasons. Historians still discuss it.
challenging.context: Aryabhata explained eclipses with shadows in 499 CE. A later astronomer, Brahmagupta, argued with him. This card asks why.

big_questions.q: The Moon is always a whole round ball, but we call it 'new', 'half' and 'full'. What other things do we name by how they look to us, not by what they are?
big_questions.hint: Think of the 'rising' Sun, or calling a person by one thing they did once.

big_questions.q: If you stood on the Moon on the night of Amavasya, what would the Earth look like in your sky?
big_questions.hint: On Amavasya, the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun. Which side of the Earth faces the Moon?

big_questions.q: The Moon's pull is slowly slowing the Earth's spin. What would life be like if a day lasted much longer?
big_questions.hint: Long ago, days were shorter. Fossil corals from about 400 million years ago grew about 400 daily layers in a year.

big_questions.q: Why can everyone on the night side of the Earth see a lunar eclipse, but only people in a narrow strip see a total solar eclipse?
big_questions.hint: Which is bigger: the Earth's shadow, or the Moon's shadow?

big_questions.q: Who owns the Moon? Should any country or company be allowed to dig it up?
big_questions.hint: In 1967, many countries signed a treaty saying no country can claim the Moon. But what about companies, or people living there one day?

big_questions.q: Does the Moon matter for itself, even if nobody lived on Earth to see it?
big_questions.hint: Corals and dung beetles watch it too. And what about the Moon before there was any life at all?

big_questions.q: Aryabhata explained eclipses with shadows 1,500 years ago, but many people kept the Rahu story. Why do old stories last, even when there is a better explanation?
big_questions.hint: What does a story give people that a shadow diagram does not?

big_questions.q: Wang Zhenyi was not supposed to study, because she was a girl. How many discoveries might the world have missed because of rules like that?
big_questions.hint: Who is not allowed, or not expected, to ask questions today?

big_questions.q: The Moon was probably made from the Earth and another planet smashed together. Is the Moon a piece of the Earth? Is part of the Earth a piece of Theia?
big_questions.hint: Where does one thing end and another begin, if they were once mixed together?

big_questions.q: Some calendars count by the Sun and some by the Moon. Which is the 'real' time?
big_questions.hint: A clock, a calendar and the sky all count something. What are they each counting?

big_questions.q: One day there will be no more total solar eclipses, because the Moon is drifting away. Is it lucky that we live now?
big_questions.hint: What else might be true only in our time, and not for ever?

story.title: The Girl Who Fed the Heavenly Dog
story.note: Wang Zhenyi is real. She lived from 1768 to 1797, read her grandfather's books on astronomy, wrote an essay explaining lunar eclipses, and is remembered for a model with a lamp, a round table and a mirror. Banging drums and gongs to scare off the heavenly dog during an eclipse was a real custom in China. Her cousin Lan, the cook, the night of this eclipse and the conversations are made up.
text: On the night the heavenly dog came to eat the Moon, my cousin Zhenyi was not frightened at all. She was annoyed. 'It is late,' she said, frowning at the sky. 'It should have started already.'

I was seven that autumn. Zhenyi was sixteen, and the cleverest person in our house, though nobody was supposed to say so. Girls were meant to sew and to be quiet. Zhenyi sewed badly and was almost never quiet. She spent her afternoons in Grandfather's library, among his tall cases of books, reading about the stars.

Down in the courtyard, everyone was ready. Old Wu the cook had his biggest pan and a ladle. My uncles had the gong from the gatehouse. My mother had a little drum, and her hands were shaking. Above the roofs hung the full Moon, round and white as a steamed bun.
'When the dog bites,' my mother told me, 'we make so much noise that it spits the Moon out again. It has always worked.'
That was true. Every time anyone could remember, the dog had bitten, the people had banged their pans, and the Moon had come back.

Then I saw it. A small dark bite, on the left edge of the Moon. My breath stuck in my throat. The courtyard exploded. The gong boomed. The pan clanged. My mother's drum rattled like rain on a roof. I clapped my hands over my ears and pressed myself against Zhenyi.

She was not banging anything. She was looking at the bite through a little rolled-up tube of paper. 'Lan,' she said, close to my ear, so I could hear her over the noise. 'Look at the edge of the bite. What shape is it?'

I did not want to look. But Zhenyi always asked questions as if your answer truly mattered, so I looked. The dark part was not jagged, like teeth marks. Its edge was a smooth curve, part of a circle. A very big circle, much bigger than the Moon.
'It is round,' I said.
'Remember that,' said Zhenyi. Then she took my hand and pulled me out of the courtyard, through the moon gate, into the dark garden.

In the middle of the garden stood the little pavilion where Grandmother used to drink tea. Zhenyi had been busy there for a week. Nobody had asked what she was doing. Nobody ever asked Zhenyi anything. From the roof beam hung a lamp, burning steadily. On the floor stood the round wooden table from the kitchen, which Old Wu had been looking for all week. Beside it, on a stand, was Grandmother's round bronze mirror.

'The lamp is the Sun,' Zhenyi said. 'The table is the Earth, where we live. The mirror is the Moon. The Moon has no light of its own, Lan. It only shines because the Sun shines on it. See?' She tilted the mirror until it flashed the lamp's light onto my face, like a little Moon.

'Now, tonight is a full Moon. Where must the Moon be, for us to see its whole bright face?' She did not wait for me to answer. 'On the far side of the Earth from the Sun. Like this.' She carried the mirror round the table and set it down on the other side, away from the lamp.

The table threw a long, dark shadow across the floor of the pavilion. Zhenyi slid the mirror slowly along, until its edge touched the shadow. A dark curve crept across the shining bronze. It was a smooth curve. Part of a very big circle.
I stared. 'It's the same bite,' I whispered.

'It is the same bite,' said Zhenyi. 'There is no dog, little cousin. There never was. Tonight the Sun, the Earth and the Moon stand in a straight line. The Earth is in the middle. So the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. And the Earth is round, so its shadow has a round edge.'
'But we see the full Moon every month,' I said. 'Why doesn't the shadow bite it every month?'

Zhenyi looked at me as if I had given her a present. She lifted the mirror a hand's width higher on its stand. Now the shadow slid underneath it, and the mirror shone, whole and bright. 'Because the Moon's road is a little tilted,' she said. 'Most months it passes just above the shadow, or just below. Only sometimes does it go straight through.'
Far away in the courtyard, the gong was still booming.
'Should we tell them?' I asked.

Zhenyi was quiet for a long moment. 'I will write it down,' she said at last. 'I will write it down so clearly that anyone who can read will understand. Even someone who has been told she is not supposed to.'

We went back to the courtyard. By then the Moon was almost swallowed, and the part inside the shadow had turned a deep, dusty red, like a lantern seen through silk. My mother cried out. But I was not afraid any more. I knew that somewhere a lamp was still burning, and a round table was still throwing its shadow, and that the shadow would slide away.
I took Old Wu's ladle and banged his pan as hard as I could, and laughed. Zhenyi raised an eyebrow at me.
'It is not for the dog,' I told her. 'It is for the Moon. It's being brave.'

Slowly, the shadow slid away, exactly as it had slid across the bronze mirror in the garden. The Moon came back, round and white. In the courtyard, everyone cheered and said the noise had worked again. In the pavilion, the lamp burned all night. In the morning, Old Wu found his table, and Zhenyi began to write.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the 'bite' out of the Moon during a lunar eclipse is the Earth's own shadow. It can only happen at full Moon, when the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon. Its curved edge is a clue that the Earth is round. And it does not happen every month because the Moon's path is tilted, so it usually passes above or below the shadow. The story also asks who is allowed to ask questions, and what we owe to people who are frightened.
ask: What shape was the edge of the 'bite' on the Moon? Why was that an important clue?
In Zhenyi's model, what was the lamp, what was the table and what was the mirror?
Why did the lunar eclipse happen on a full Moon night, and not on a half Moon night?
Why doesn't an eclipse happen at every full Moon? What did Zhenyi do to the mirror to show it?
Lan banged the pan at the end, even though she knew there was no dog. Why do you think she did?
Zhenyi was not supposed to study because she was a girl. What would have been lost if she had obeyed?
art: A Chinese courtyard at night under a full Moon with a small dark bite on its edge, a family banging a gong, a pan and a drum, a teenage girl calmly looking up through a paper tube.
A small girl and her older cousin hurrying through a round moon gate into a dark garden.
A garden pavilion with a lamp hanging from the roof, a round wooden table, and a round bronze mirror with a curved shadow creeping across it.
The teenage girl lifting the mirror higher so the shadow slides underneath, the little cousin watching wide-eyed.
A red, eclipsed Moon over the courtyard, the little girl laughing and banging a pan, and the older cousin at a desk at dawn, writing.

rules: Cut out the 16 cards. Shuffle them and lay them face down in a 4 by 4 square.

With friends or a parent, the player with the most pairs wins. Playing alone, time yourself finding all 8 pairs and filling the ring. Next time, try to beat your time.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards and the ring. 2. Shuffle the 16 cards and lay them face down in a 4 by 4 square. 3. Put the ring to one side.
flow.say: This is a memory game about the Moon's shapes. A pair is a picture of the Moon and the clue that tells you when you see it.
flow.kid: Mix up the 16 cards. Lay them face down in 4 rows of 4. A pair is one Moon picture and its clue.
flow.context: This is the first step of Moon Pairs. It is a memory card game about the Moon's shapes, called phases, and when you can see each one.

flow.do: Play one practice turn together. Turn over the Full Moon picture and the Purnima clue, face up, and match them.
flow.say: Here is a practice pair. The full Moon picture goes with the Purnima clue. Why does the full Moon rise just as the Sun sets?
flow.kid: Practice pair: the full Moon and the Purnima clue. Why does the full Moon rise as the Sun sets? Tap your answer.

check.q: Why does the full Moon rise just as the Sun sets?
options: The full Moon is on the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun
The Moon waits for the Sun to go to sleep
The full Moon is closest to the Sun
check.why: At full Moon, the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon. So the Moon is on the opposite side of our sky from the Sun. As the Sun sinks in the west, the Moon comes up in the east. Picking 'closest to the Sun' usually comes from thinking a brighter Moon must be nearer the light. In fact, the full Moon is the furthest from the Sun of all the phases.

flow.do: 1. Put the practice cards back face down and shuffle the square again. 2. Take turns turning over two cards. 3. Keep a pair only if the player can say why the cards match.
flow.say: Turn over two cards. If they match, tell us why.
flow.kid: Turn over two cards. Do they match? Say why. If they match, keep them and go again.
flow.parent: The trickiest pairs are the growing and shrinking ones. In India, a growing Moon is lit on its right, the side towards the setting Sun. A shrinking Moon is lit on its left. A growing Moon is seen in the evening. A shrinking Moon is best seen late at night or in the morning.

flow.do: When all pairs are found, put the 8 picture cards on the ring in order. Start with the new Moon at space 1, between the Earth and the Sun.
flow.say: Now put the Moons round the ring in the order they come. Where does the full Moon go?
flow.kid: Put the 8 Moon pictures round the ring in order. Start with the new Moon next to the Sun. Where does the full Moon go?

check.q: On the ring, where does the full Moon go?
options: Space 5, on the far side of the Earth from the Sun
Space 1, between the Earth and the Sun
Space 3, at the side
check.why: We see the whole lit half only when the Moon is on the far side of us from the Sun, at space 5. At space 1 the lit half faces away, so it is the new Moon. Picking space 1 usually means thinking the Moon is brightest when nearest the Sun. At space 3 it is a half Moon.

flow.think: The ring is round, and the month starts again after space 8. What else in your life goes round in a circle like this?

games.context: This is a memory card game. Each pair is a picture of one Moon shape and a clue saying when you see it. At the end you put the Moon shapes in order round a ring.

BELOW: the Moon passes below the line

rules: Each player puts a Moon token on space 1, the new Moon. Shuffle the 10 tilt cards and put them face down.
On your turn, roll the dice and move your Moon that many spaces round the ring.
Say the name of the Moon shape you land on.

Each time your Moon lands on or passes space 1 (New Moon) or space 5 (Full Moon), turn over a tilt card. If it says ON THE LINE, there is an eclipse! At space 1 take a solar eclipse card. At space 5 take a lunar eclipse card. Say who on Earth can see it. Then shuffle the tilt card back in.
With friends or a parent, the first player to catch 2 eclipses wins. Playing alone, go round the ring 5 times, count how many eclipses you catch, and then try to beat your score.

flow.do: 1. Put the board in the middle. 2. Shuffle the tilt cards face down. 3. Each player puts a token on space 1, the new Moon.
flow.say: Your token is the Moon going round the Earth. You can only catch an eclipse when the Sun, the Earth and the Moon are in a line. Where on the ring could that happen?
flow.kid: Your token is the Moon. It goes round the Earth. An eclipse needs the Sun, the Earth and the Moon in a line. Where could that be?
flow.context: This is the first step of Eclipse Hunters. It is a board game where your Moon goes round the Earth, and you try to catch eclipses. An eclipse is when the Earth or the Moon throws its shadow onto the other.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to roll the dice and move. 2. Name the Moon shape you land on. 3. Each time your Moon lands on or passes space 1 or space 5, turn over a tilt card.
flow.say: You landed on the full Moon! Turn a tilt card. Is the Moon on the line this month?
flow.kid: Roll and move. Name your Moon shape. Reach or pass new Moon or full Moon? Turn a tilt card. ON THE LINE means an eclipse!

ask.q: You turned ABOVE on a full Moon. Why is there no eclipse?
good: The Moon passed above the Earth's shadow.
The Moon's path is tilted, so the shadow missed it.

ask.q: You caught a lunar eclipse. Who on Earth can see it?
good: Everyone on the night side of the Earth.
Everyone who can see the Moon at that time.

flow.parent: Every Moon passes new Moon and full Moon once a lap, just as the real Moon does every month. Only 2 of the 10 tilt cards say ON THE LINE, so most new and full Moons have no eclipse. That is true of the real sky. In the real sky, eclipses also come in 'seasons', about six months apart, when the line through Rahu and Ketu points towards the Sun.

flow.do: The first time a player catches a solar eclipse, stop and ask this question.
flow.say: If you catch a solar eclipse, can everyone on Earth see it?
flow.kid: You caught a solar eclipse! Can everyone on Earth see it? Tap your answer.

check.q: In a total solar eclipse, who sees the Sun fully covered?
options: Only people in a narrow strip where the Moon's dark shadow falls
Everyone on the daytime side of the Earth
Everyone on the whole Earth
check.why: The Moon is much smaller than the Earth, so its darkest shadow only covers a small patch of the Earth. Only people in that patch see the Sun fully covered. People nearby see part of the Sun covered. In a lunar eclipse it is different: the Earth's big shadow covers the whole Moon, so everyone who can see the Moon sees it. Picking 'the daytime side' usually means mixing up the two kinds of eclipse.

flow.do: Count the eclipse cards and find the winner. Then count how many times anyone passed new or full Moon without an eclipse.
flow.say: How many times did someone pass a new or full Moon with no eclipse? Why are eclipses so rare?
flow.kid: Count your eclipse cards. How many times did you pass new or full Moon with no eclipse? Why?
flow.think: People long ago were frightened by eclipses because they seemed to come from nowhere. Once you know the rule, are they less amazing, or more?
