items.p: Where does moonlight come from?
opts: The Moon makes its own light
items.why: The Moon makes no light. It shines because sunlight bounces off it. Picking 'makes its own light' is natural, because it glows so brightly in the dark. But on Amavasya, when the lit side faces away, we see nothing at all.

items.p: Why does the Moon seem to change shape?
opts: The Earth's shadow covers part of it
We see more or less of its sunlit half as it goes round us
items.why: Half the Moon is always lit. As it goes round the Earth, we see different amounts of that lit half. Picking 'the Earth's shadow' is the most common wrong idea. The Earth's shadow only reaches the Moon in a lunar eclipse.
items.art: The Moon in four places round the Earth, with sunlight coming from one side.

items.p: Put these Moon shapes in the order they come after Amavasya: full Moon, growing half Moon, thin crescent, gibbous Moon.
items.why: After Amavasya, the lit part grows: first a thin crescent, then a half, then a gibbous, then full.

items.p: The night when we cannot see the Moon at all is called new Moon, or ____ in Hindi.
items.why: Amavasya is the new Moon. The Moon's lit half faces away from us, towards the Sun.

items.p: The full Moon night is called ____.
items.why: Purnima is the full Moon, when we see all of the Moon's lit half.

items.p: From one new Moon to the next takes about ____ days.
items.why: A lunar month is about 29 and a half days. Calendars give lunar months 29 or 30 days.

items.p: The far side of the Moon is always dark.
items.why: False. The far side gets just as much sunlight as the side we see. We just never see it from the Earth. On Amavasya, the far side is in full daylight.

items.p: The Moon spins round once for each trip it makes round the Earth.
items.why: True. That is why we always see the same face. Walking round a chair while facing it shows it: you face every wall once.

items.p: Remember the ball and lamp experiment. Where was the ball when you saw a full Moon?
opts: On the far side of you from the lamp
Right on top of the lamp
items.why: You saw the whole lit face only with the lamp behind you. So a full Moon is on the far side of the Earth from the Sun. Picking 'between you and the lamp' gives the new Moon, when the lit side faces away.
items.context: This question is about the ball and lamp experiment. A lamp is the Sun, a pale ball on a pencil is the Moon, and your head is the Earth. You turn slowly and watch the ball's lit part.

items.p: Match each Moon to when it rises.
items.why: The Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day. The full Moon is opposite the Sun, so it rises as the Sun sets. The new Moon is next to the Sun, so it rises with it.

items.p: Sort these festivals: set by the Moon, or set by the Sun?
items.why: Moon festivals fall on a tithi, like Amavasya or Purnima, so their dates move each year. Sun festivals, like Makar Sankranti and Pongal, stay on nearly the same date.

items.p: A lunar eclipse can only happen on…
items.why: In a lunar eclipse, the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. That needs the Earth to be between the Sun and the Moon, which only happens at full Moon. Picking 'new Moon' means mixing it up with a solar eclipse, which happens at new Moon.

items.p: In the evening, a growing Moon seen from India is lit on which side?
opts: The right side, towards where the Sun set
items.why: The lit side always faces the Sun. In the evening, the Sun has set in the west, which is to the right of the Moon when you face it. Picking 'the left' gives a shrinking Moon, which is best seen late at night or in the morning.
items.context: A Moon diary is a record of the Moon's shape, the date, the time and the direction, kept night after night.

items.p: The bright half of the month, when the Moon grows, is called Shukla ____.
items.why: Shukla Paksha is the bright half. Krishna Paksha is the dark half, when the Moon shrinks.

items.p: Your friend says the Moon only comes out at night. What would you tell them? Give one example.
items.a: The Moon is in the sky in the daytime for about half of each month. For example, a few days after Purnima you can see it in the morning sky in the west.
items.why: Any answer that says the Moon is up in the daytime on some days, with an example, is right.

items.p: Draw the Moon on the night of your favourite Moon festival. Write the festival's name and whether it is Amavasya or Purnima.
items.a: For example, Diwali: a dark sky with no Moon, because it is Amavasya. Or Holi: a full round Moon, because it is Purnima.
items.why: Diwali falls on Amavasya, Holi on Purnima.
items.art: An empty night sky box above a row of rooftops.

items.p: Why do we always see the same face of the Moon?
opts: The Moon spins exactly once for each trip round the Earth
The other side is too dark to see
items.why: The Moon spins once every 27 and a third days, exactly the time of one trip round us. So it keeps its face towards us. Picking 'does not spin' is the most common idea. But if it didn't spin, we would see all its sides during a month.

items.p: What slowed the young Moon's spin until it matched its trip round the Earth?
opts: The Earth's pull on a slight bulge in the Moon's rock, acting like a brake
items.why: The Earth's gravity stretched the Moon into a very slight bulge. As the Moon spun, the Earth kept tugging the bulge back, like a brake. Picking 'air' is a good guess, since friction slows things. But the Moon has almost no air.

items.p: Remember the walk round the chair. You walked round it, always facing it. What did you find?
opts: I faced every wall once, so I turned round once
items.why: Your face pointed at every wall in turn, so you turned round once. The Moon does the same each trip round the Earth.
items.context: In this activity you walk round a chair as if you were the Moon, always facing the chair, which is the Earth.

items.p: Remember the shadow experiment. Which shadow could cover the whole of the other ball?
opts: The football's shadow covered the whole lime
The lime's shadow covered the whole football
items.why: The football is far bigger, so its shadow can swallow the lime. The lime only makes a small spot on the football. So everyone who can see the Moon sees a lunar eclipse, but only people in a narrow strip see a total solar eclipse.
items.context: This question is about the shadow experiment. A torch is the Sun, a football is the Earth and a lime is the Moon.

items.p: Why don't we get an eclipse every full Moon?
opts: The Moon's path is tilted, so it usually passes above or below the Earth's shadow
The Moon is too far away at full Moon
items.why: The Moon's path is tilted about 5 degrees. Most months it misses the shadow. Eclipses only happen when the full or new Moon is near the two crossing points, which Indian astronomers named Rahu and Ketu.

items.p: Everyone on the whole Earth can see a total solar eclipse at the same time.
items.why: False. The Moon's dark shadow only covers a small patch of the Earth. People nearby see a partial eclipse, and people far away see nothing.

items.p: It is safe to watch a lunar eclipse with your bare eyes.
items.why: True. The Moon is not bright enough to hurt your eyes. Only the Sun is dangerous. Never look straight at the Sun, during an eclipse or at any other time.

items.p: In a total lunar eclipse, the Moon often turns a coppery ____ colour.
items.why: A little sunlight bends through the Earth's air. The air lets red light through and scatters blue away, the same way sunsets are red.

items.p: Match each person to what they did.
pairs: made an eclipse model with a lamp, a table and a mirror
first photographs of the far side
items.why: Aryabhata wrote about shadows in the Aryabhatiya. Wang Zhenyi built her model in China. Leonardo explained earthshine in his notebooks. Luna 3 was a Soviet spacecraft.

items.p: What is earthshine? Where does its light come from?
items.a: Earthshine is the faint glow on the dark part of a crescent Moon. Sunlight bounces off the Earth onto the Moon, and then back to our eyes.
items.why: The light travels from the Sun to the Earth, to the Moon, and back to us.

items.p: A tithi in the Indian calendar is…
opts: A Moon day. There are 30 in each lunar month.
A Sun day of exactly 24 hours
items.why: A tithi is a Moon day. It can be a few hours shorter or longer than a Sun day, because the Moon's speed changes. Picking 'exactly 24 hours' mixes it up with a clock day.

items.p: Why do Indian calendars add an extra month, adhik maas, about once every three years?
opts: So that festivals stay in the same season
Because the Moon goes faster in some years
items.why: Twelve Moon months make about 354 days, 11 days short of a Sun year. After three years that is more than a month. The extra month brings the calendar back in step with the seasons.

items.p: Remember the rising Moon experiment. The full Moon looked huge as it rose. What did the masoor dal show?
opts: It was the same size, rising and high
It was much bigger when rising
It was much bigger when high
items.why: The dal covered the Moon the same way both times. The rising Moon only looks bigger. That is the Moon illusion, made by our brains.
items.context: In this experiment you hide the full Moon behind a masoor dal held at arm's length, once as it rises and again when it is high.

items.p: Sort these: something we can see from India, or something only astronauts or spacecraft have seen?
cats: Only seen from space or the Moon
items: the far side of the Moon
Only seen from space or the Moon
Only seen from space or the Moon
a red Moon in an eclipse
items.why: We always see the near side of the Moon from the Earth. The far side, and the Earth's own phases, can only be seen from space.

items.p: Draw a lunar eclipse from the side: the Sun, the Earth with its shadow, and the Moon inside the shadow. Label each one.
items.a: The Sun on one side, the Earth in the middle, a long dark shadow behind the Earth, and the Moon inside that shadow, all in a straight line.
items.why: In a lunar eclipse the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, so the Moon is inside the Earth's shadow.
items.art: An empty box with a small Sun drawn at the left edge.

items.p: If you stood on the Moon on the night of Amavasya, what would the Earth look like?
items.why: On Amavasya, the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun. So the side of the Earth facing the Moon is in daylight. From the Moon, you would see a nearly full Earth. Picking 'completely dark' means thinking the Earth and Moon always have the same phase. In fact their phases are opposite.

items.p: The Moon goes once round the Earth, measured against the stars, in about 27 and a third days. Why does new Moon to new Moon take about 29 and a half days?
opts: The Earth moves along its path round the Sun, so the Moon needs about two more days to line up again
The Moon slows down near the Sun
items.why: While the Moon goes round us, we also move round the Sun. So the Moon must go a little further to get back between us and the Sun. Picking 'calendars round it up' is a fair guess, but the difference is real: it is about two whole days.

items.p: How do scientists know the Moon is moving away from the Earth?
opts: They bounce laser light off mirrors left on the Moon and time it
They measure it with a very long tape
items.why: Astronauts left mirrors on the Moon. Scientists fire lasers at them and time how long the light takes to come back. The Moon moves about 3.8 centimetres further away every year.

items.p: Moon rocks brought back by astronauts are very like the rock of the Earth's outer layers. Which idea about the Moon's birth does this fit best?
opts: A giant crash splashed out rock from the young Earth
The Moon was a wandering planet that the Earth caught
The Moon formed far away and drifted here
items.why: A crash that splashed out the Earth's outer rock would make a Moon of very similar rock. A captured wanderer would probably be made of different rock. The puzzle scientists still argue about is why the match is so close.

items.p: Scientists all agree on exactly how the Moon was made.
items.why: False. Most think a giant crash made it, but they argue about the details: one crash or many, and whether the Moon formed in years or in hours.

items.p: Indian astronomers named the two points where the Moon's path crosses the Sun's path Rahu and Ketu. What happens when a full Moon falls near one of them?
opts: There can be a lunar eclipse
items.why: Near those points, the Sun, the Earth and the Moon can line up exactly. At full Moon, the Earth's shadow then falls on the Moon. The old names from the Rahu story were kept for something astronomers could calculate.

items.p: In 1868, a new element was found in the light of a solar eclipse seen from Guntur in India. What was it?
items.why: Jules Janssen saw a strange yellow line in the light of the Sun's edge. Norman Lockyer said it was a new element and named it helium, after Helios, the Greek word for the Sun.

items.p: The Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day. Purnima's Moon rose at 6 in the evening. Two days later it will rise at about ____.
items.why: 50 minutes plus 50 minutes is 100 minutes, which is 1 hour and 40 minutes. 6 o'clock plus 1 hour and 40 minutes is 7:40.

items.p: Twelve Moon months make about 354 days. A Sun year is 365 days. After 3 years, a Moon calendar is about ____ days behind.
items.why: 365 minus 354 is 11 days a year. 11 times 3 is 33 days. That is more than one whole Moon month, so an extra month is added.

items.p: Many corals on the Great Barrier Reef release their eggs on the same few nights each year. What sets the timing?
opts: The full Moon in late spring, sensed through moonlight
items.why: Corals spawn together on a few nights after a full Moon, when the water has warmed. Each coral polyp seems to sense the moonlight. Releasing eggs all together helps them meet.

items.p: Scientists have proved that the full Moon makes people behave strangely.
items.why: False. Large studies of hospitals and police records found no real link. A few studies suggest people sleep a little less before a full Moon, but others disagree.

items.p: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and about 400 times further away. What does this mean?
opts: They look about the same size in our sky, so the Moon can just cover the Sun
The Sun is smaller than the Moon
items.why: Something 400 times wider but also 400 times further away looks the same size. So in a total solar eclipse, the Moon just covers the Sun. As the Moon drifts away, this perfect fit will not last for ever.

items.p: Wang Zhenyi was not supposed to study, because she was a girl. She explained eclipses anyway. Why do you think it matters who is allowed to do science?
items.a: Any thoughtful answer. For example: if only some people may ask questions, many good answers are never found. Everyone notices different things.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A good answer gives a reason.

items.p: The Earth's pull slowed the Moon's spin, and the Moon's pull is slowing the Earth's spin. Is the Earth in charge of the Moon, or are they partners? Explain.
items.a: Any thoughtful answer. For example: they are partners, because each changes the other. The Earth locked the Moon's face, and the Moon makes our tides and slows our days. They both go round a point between them.
items.why: A good answer uses at least one way each one changes the other.

items.p: Design a Moon base on the far side of the Moon. Show how it would talk to the Earth.
items.a: Any design that includes a relay satellite or another way to send messages round the Moon.
items.why: The whole Moon blocks a straight line from the far side to the Earth, so a relay is needed.
items.art: An empty box with the far side of the Moon drawn as a curve at the bottom.

experiments.title: Make Every Moon: a ball, a lamp and your head
experiments.question: Why does the Moon seem to change shape during the month?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Draw what you think the ball will look like when it is between you and the lamp. Then draw what it will look like when it is behind you, away from the lamp. Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Keep everything the same except where the ball is. Use one lamp that stays still, the same ball, and always hold it at arm's length, a little above your head. Only turn yourself to move the ball round.
results_table: Lit on the left, the right, all or none?

materials.item: a mobile phone torch propped on a table or a pile of books at head height, or one bright lamp with its shade taken off
a pale round fruit about the size of an orange, like a mosambi or an orange, with a pencil pushed into it as a handle
a room you can make dark, with space to turn round (after sunset, or with the curtains closed)
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: A bare bulb gets hot. Do not touch it, and keep it away from curtains. If you use a phone torch, do not stare into it.

schedule.what: Guess. Make the new Moon, the growing Moons, the full Moon and the shrinking Moons. Try an eclipse. Fill in the table.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw the 8 Moon shapes round a circle, in the order you saw them.

flow.do: 1. Put the lamp at one end of the room, at about the height of your child's head. 2. Push the ball onto the pencil. 3. Make the room as dark as you can, with only the lamp on. 4. Your child stands about 2 big steps from the lamp, facing it.
flow.say: This lamp is the Sun. Your head is the Earth, and your eyes are you, standing on the Earth. This ball is the Moon. Hold it out at arm's length, a little higher than your head.
flow.kid: The lamp is the Sun. Your head is the Earth. The ball is the Moon. Stand two big steps from the lamp. Hold the ball out at arm's length, a bit above your head.
flow.parent: The room must be dark, apart from the lamp. One bright light works much better than a room full of soft light, because it gives a sharp edge between the lit and dark halves. If the edge looks blurry, move closer to the lamp.
flow.context: This is the first step of Make Every Moon. You use a lamp as the Sun, a ball as the Moon and your own head as the Earth, to make all the Moon's shapes.

flow.do: Your child holds the ball straight out towards the lamp, a little above it. They look at the side of the ball facing them.
flow.say: Now the Moon is between you and the Sun. Look at the side of the ball facing you. How much of it is lit?
flow.kid: Hold the ball towards the lamp, a bit above it. Look at the side facing you. Can you see any light on it?

good: It's on the other side, facing the lamp.
The lit half is facing away from me.

flow.parent: Your child should see a dark ball against the bright lamp. This is the new Moon, Amavasya. The lit half faces the Sun, away from us.

flow.do: 1. Your child turns slowly to their left, on the spot, keeping the ball at arm's length in front of their face. 2. Stop when the lamp is at their right side. 3. Keep turning until their back is to the lamp. 4. Each time, look at the ball and name the shape.
flow.say: Turn slowly to your left. Watch the ball. What happens to the bright part? Stop when the lamp is at your right side. Now keep turning until the lamp is behind you.
flow.kid: Turn slowly to your left. Keep looking at the ball. Watch the light grow! Stop when the lamp is at your right side. Then keep turning until the lamp is behind you.

ask.q: Which side of the ball is lit as it starts to grow, left or right?

flow.parent: Your child will see a thin crescent lit on the right, then a half Moon when the lamp is at their right side, then a fat gibbous Moon, then a full Moon with the lamp behind them. That is the real order of a growing Moon seen from India. If the full Moon goes dark, the shadow of their head is falling on it. Lift the ball a little higher. That dark moment is a lunar eclipse, which you will try on purpose in a later step.

flow.do: Keep turning left, all the way round, until your child faces the lamp again.
flow.say: Keep turning. What happens to the light now? Which side is lit this time?
flow.kid: Keep turning left, all the way round. Watch the light shrink. Which side is lit now?

check.q: When you could see the whole lit face of the ball, a full Moon, where was the ball?
options: On the far side of me from the lamp
Between me and the lamp
Right next to the lamp
check.why: You see the whole lit half only when you are between the lamp and the ball, looking at the side the lamp shines on. So a full Moon is on the far side of the Earth from the Sun. Picking 'between me and the lamp' usually means thinking the Moon is brightest when it is nearest the Sun. That is the new Moon, when we see nothing.

flow.do: 1. Your child turns until the lamp is behind them again, for a full Moon. 2. They lower the ball slowly, until it is exactly level with their head.
flow.say: Lower the ball until it is exactly in line with your head and the lamp. What happens?
flow.kid: Lamp behind you. Full Moon in front. Now lower the ball until it is level with your head. What happens?
flow.parent: The ball goes dark, because the shadow of your child's head falls on it. That is a lunar eclipse: the Earth's shadow on the Moon. Most months the real Moon passes a little above or below the shadow, just as the ball did when you held it higher. That is why we don't get an eclipse every full Moon.
flow.think: If you put the ball between your eyes and the lamp, exactly in line, what would happen to the lamp? What kind of eclipse would that be?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things about what you found. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the Moon doesn't really change shape. What I saw: half of the ball was always lit, and as I turned, I saw more or less of the lit half. Why: the Sun always lights half the Moon, and as the Moon goes round us we see different amounts of that half.

experiments.context: In this experiment you use a lamp as the Sun, a ball as the Moon and your head as the Earth. Turning slowly, you make every shape the Moon goes through in a month.

experiments.title: Which Shadow Is Bigger? Wang Zhenyi's eclipses at home
experiments.question: Why can everyone on the night side of the Earth see a lunar eclipse, but only a few people see a total solar eclipse?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the small ball's shadow cover the whole big ball? Will the big ball's shadow cover the whole small ball? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Keep the torch, the two balls and the gap between the balls the same. Change only which ball is nearer the torch. Measure the shadow each time with a ruler.
results_table: How wide the dark shadow is (cm)
How much of the other ball is covered

materials.item: a small bright torch, or a mobile phone torch
a big ball for the Earth, like a football
a small ball for the Moon, about a quarter as wide, like a lime, with a pencil pushed into it as a handle
a ruler
a table in a dark room

experiments.safety: Do not shine the torch into anyone's eyes.

schedule.what: Make a solar eclipse and a lunar eclipse with two balls and a torch. Measure the shadows.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw both eclipses from the side, with the torch, the two balls and the shadows.

flow.do: 1. Put the football on a bowl or a roll of tape so it does not roll. 2. Put the torch on a pile of books about 2 metres away, shining at the football. 3. Darken the room.
flow.say: About 240 years ago, a young woman in China called Wang Zhenyi made eclipses. She used a lamp, a round table and a mirror. We will use a torch and two balls. The torch is the Sun. The football is the Earth. The lime is the Moon.
flow.kid: Wang Zhenyi made eclipses in her garden about 240 years ago. Now you will too. The torch is the Sun. The football is the Earth. The lime is the Moon.
flow.parent: A small, bright torch gives sharp shadows. A big lamp gives blurry ones, because its light comes from many directions. If your shadows look fuzzy, move the torch further away.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Which Shadow Is Bigger experiment. You build a model of eclipses, like the one Wang Zhenyi made in China about 240 years ago.

flow.do: 1. Hold the lime between the torch and the football, about 30 centimetres from the football. 2. Move it until its shadow falls on the football. 3. Measure how wide the dark spot is with the ruler.
flow.say: This is a solar eclipse. The Moon is between the Sun and the Earth. Look at the Earth. How much of it is in the Moon's shadow?
flow.kid: Hold the lime between the torch and the football. Find its shadow on the football. Measure the dark spot. Is the whole football dark?

ask.q: If you were a tiny person on the football, where would you have to stand to see the torch blocked?
good: Only in the shadow, not on the rest of the ball.

flow.do: 1. Move the lime to the far side of the football, about 30 centimetres behind it. 2. Move it into the football's shadow. 3. Look at how much of the lime is dark.
flow.say: Now this is a lunar eclipse. The Earth is between the Sun and the Moon. How much of the Moon is in the Earth's shadow?
flow.kid: Move the lime behind the football, into its shadow. How much of the lime goes dark?

check.q: Which shadow could cover the whole of the other ball?
options: The football's shadow covered the whole lime
The lime's shadow covered the whole football
Both covered the whole of the other ball
check.why: The football is much bigger than the lime, so its shadow is big enough to swallow the lime whole. The lime's shadow only makes a small spot on the football. That is why everyone who can see the Moon can see a lunar eclipse, but only people in a small patch see a total solar eclipse. Picking 'both' usually means thinking shadows are always the same size as each other.

flow.do: Keep the lime behind the football, but lift it slowly, about 15 to 20 centimetres, until it comes out of the shadow.
flow.say: Now the Moon passes a little above the shadow. Is there an eclipse?
flow.kid: Lift the lime slowly. When does it come out of the shadow? This is what the real Moon does most months.
flow.parent: The real Moon's path is tilted a little. So most months, it passes above or below the Earth's shadow, and there is no eclipse. In space, the Moon's darkest shadow is even smaller than in this model. The Sun is far bigger than the Moon, so that shadow narrows as it goes. By the time it reaches the Earth, it is a spot at most about 270 kilometres wide. Your torch is smaller than the lime, so here the shadow spreads out instead.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things about what you found. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the Earth's shadow is much bigger than the Moon's shadow. What I saw: the lime's shadow made a spot about 7 cm wide on the football, but the football's shadow covered the whole lime. Why: the Earth is nearly four times as wide as the Moon, so it throws a much bigger shadow.

experiments.context: In this experiment you make a solar eclipse and a lunar eclipse with a torch, a football and a lime. You find out which shadow is bigger, and who can see each kind of eclipse.

experiments.title: Is the Rising Moon Really Bigger?
experiments.question: Is the full Moon really bigger when it is rising than when it is high in the sky?
experiments.predict: Guess first. When you measure the rising Moon and the high Moon, will the rising Moon be bigger, smaller or the same? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Use the same masoor dal, held at the same distance from your eye, with your arm straight both times. Change only how high the Moon is.
results_table: Does it look big or small?
Does the dal cover it exactly, with room to spare, or not quite?

materials.item: one whole masoor dal (a red lentil), about half a centimetre wide
a window, balcony or terrace that looks east
a calendar or app that shows the date of Purnima
a phone camera, if you have one

experiments.safety: Watch from a window or a balcony if you can. On a terrace, go only with a grown-up and stay well away from the edges.

schedule.what: On Purnima, or the night after, look at the Moon as it rises. Measure it. Measure again two or three hours later.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the Moon next to the horizon and high in the sky, both drawn the size you measured.

flow.do: 1. Find the date of Purnima on a calendar. 2. That evening, or the evening after, go to an east-facing window or balcony at sunset. 3. Look east and wait for the Moon to rise.
flow.say: The full Moon rises in the east, just as the Sun sets in the west. Let's watch for it. How big does it look?
flow.kid: On Purnima, look east at sunset with a grown-up. Watch for the Moon to rise. How big does it look?
flow.parent: The full Moon rises close to sunset. The night after Purnima it rises about 50 minutes later. In a city, buildings will hide it at first. That is fine: it still looks huge when it first shows above the rooftops. In the monsoon, clouds may hide it. Then try again next month.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Is the Rising Moon Really Bigger experiment. On a full Moon night, you measure the Moon as it rises, and again later when it is high.

flow.do: 1. Hold the masoor dal between your finger and thumb. 2. Stretch your arm out straight. 3. Close one eye. 4. Move the dal in front of the Moon and see whether it covers it.
flow.say: Hold the dal at the end of your straight arm. Close one eye. Can you hide the whole Moon behind it?
flow.kid: Hold one dal at the end of your straight arm. Close one eye. Try to hide the Moon behind the dal. Does it fit?

ask.q: Did it fit? Were you surprised?
good: Yes, the tiny dal covered the whole Moon.
I thought the Moon was much bigger than that.

flow.parent: At arm's length, a masoor dal just covers the full Moon, or nearly does. Most people are amazed at how small the Moon really is in the sky. If you have a phone, take a photo without zooming, and keep it.

flow.do: 1. Two or three hours later, go back to the same window or balcony. 2. Measure the Moon the same way, with a straight arm and one eye closed. 3. If you have a phone, take another photo without zooming.
flow.wait: Wait two or three hours, until the Moon is high in the sky.
flow.say: The Moon is high now. Does it look smaller? Let's measure it with the same dal.
flow.kid: Look again when the Moon is high. Does it look smaller? Measure it the same way.

options: The Moon was the same size both times
The rising Moon was much bigger
The high Moon was much bigger
check.why: The dal covered the Moon just the same both times, so the Moon was the same size in the sky. The rising Moon only looks bigger. This is called the Moon illusion, and it happens in our brains, not in the sky. Picking 'the rising Moon was much bigger' means trusting what it looks like over what we measured. That is exactly the trap the measuring helps us escape.

flow.do: If you took two photos, put them side by side and compare the size of the Moon in each.
flow.say: The photos agree with the dal. The camera doesn't have a brain to fool. So why does the rising Moon look so big to us?
flow.kid: Look at your two photos. Is the Moon the same size? The camera is not fooled. Why are we?
flow.think: Scientists have argued about the Moon illusion for more than 2,000 years. Nobody is sure why it happens. What do you think? Does seeing trees and houses next to the Moon change how big it looks?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things about what you found. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the rising Moon is not really bigger. What I saw: the same dal covered the Moon when it was rising and when it was high, and my two photos showed the same size. Why: the Moon stays the same distance away, so it is my brain that makes the rising Moon look bigger.

experiments.context: On a full Moon night, the rising Moon looks huge. In this experiment you measure it with a masoor dal held at arm's length, as it rises and again when it is high, to see if it really changes size.

activities.title: Walk Round the Chair: does the Moon spin?

materials.item: a chair in the middle of a room, and a sticky note or a bindi

activities.safety: Walk slowly. Move anything you could trip over first.

schedule.what: Walk round a chair as the Moon, always facing it. Count the walls you faced.

activities.record: Draw the chair from above, with you at four places round it, and an arrow for the way your nose pointed each time.

flow.do: 1. Put a chair in the middle of the room. It is the Earth. 2. Stick a sticky note or a bindi on your child's forehead. It marks the Moon's face. 3. Your child stands a big step from the chair, facing it.
flow.say: You are the Moon. The chair is the Earth. The sticker is the face we always see. Walk all the way round the chair, slowly, and always keep your sticker facing the chair.
flow.kid: You are the Moon. The chair is the Earth. Put a sticker on your forehead. Walk slowly round the chair. Keep your sticker facing the chair all the time.
flow.context: This is the first step of Walk Round the Chair. You act as the Moon going round the Earth, to find out whether the Moon spins.

flow.do: As your child walks round, call out the name of each wall or window they are facing. When they get back to the start, ask how many walls they faced.
flow.say: What are you looking at now, behind the chair? And now? When you got back to the start, how many walls had your face pointed at?
flow.kid: As you walk, look past the chair. What wall can you see? Keep going round. How many walls did you face, by the end?

check.q: You walked round the chair, always facing it. Did you turn round?
options: Yes, I turned round once, because I faced every wall
No, I didn't turn at all
I turned round four times
check.why: Your face pointed at every wall of the room, one after another. So you turned round once while you went round the chair once. The Moon does the same. It spins once for each trip round the Earth, so the Earth always sees its same face. Picking 'I didn't turn' is the most common answer, because the chair always saw the same side of you.

flow.do: 1. Now your child walks round the chair again, but this time always faces the same wall, without turning. 2. Ask what the chair can see of them.
flow.say: Now go round again, but don't turn at all. Always face the door. What does the chair see now?
flow.kid: Go round again. This time always face the door. Don't turn. What does the chair see now? Your face, your side or your back?
flow.parent: If the Moon did not spin at all, the Earth would see all of its sides during a month, front, side, back and other side. We only see one face because the Moon spins exactly once each trip. Long ago it spun faster. The Earth's pull on a slight bulge in the Moon's rock worked like a brake, until the spin matched the trip. This is called tidal locking.
flow.think: What if the Moon spun twice for each trip round the Earth? Try it round the chair. Would we see its far side?

activities.context: In this activity you walk round a chair as if you were the Moon going round the Earth. It shows why we always see the same face of the Moon, and whether the Moon spins.

activities.title: Moon Diary: from Amavasya to Purnima and beyond

materials.item: a window, balcony or terrace you can look out of after sunset. The Moon moves across the sky, so you may use a west window early on and an east window near Purnima.
a notebook or the printed diary page, with a box for each night
a pencil
a calendar that marks Amavasya and Purnima, or a free Moon-phase website
a watch or a phone to note the time
binoculars, if you have them

activities.safety: Watch from a window or balcony if you can. On a terrace, go only with a grown-up after dark and stay away from the edges. Never point binoculars anywhere near the Sun.

schedule.what: Two or three days after Amavasya, just after sunset, look low in the west. Draw the thin crescent, the buildings under it, the date and the time. Look for earthshine.
Same place, same time. Draw the Moon again. Is it bigger? Has it moved?
Same time. It should be about half, high in the south. Look along its straight edge with binoculars, if you have them, for mountains and craters.
Same time. Draw the Moon. Which direction do you face to see it now?
Same time. Draw the gibbous Moon, now lower in the south-east.
Same time. Draw the Moon. Is it nearly full?
Purnima (check the calendar: it may be a day either side). At sunset look east and watch the full Moon rise. Draw it and note the time.
The night after Purnima. At the same time as yesterday, is the Moon up yet? Note when it rises, if you can.
In the morning, before or on the way to school, look west for the shrinking Moon. Then lay all your drawings in a row and find the pattern.

activities.record: One box for each night you looked: the date, the time, the direction you faced, the Moon's shape drawn carefully, and whether it was lit on the left or the right. Leave cloudy nights as a box marked 'cloudy'.

flow.do: 1. Find the date of the next Amavasya on a calendar. 2. Two or three days later, go to a west-facing window or balcony just after sunset. 3. Look low in the sky, where the Sun went down, for a thin crescent. 4. Draw it with the buildings under it, and write the date and time.
flow.say: We'll keep a Moon diary for about two weeks. Tonight the Moon is a thin crescent, close to where the Sun set. Which side of it is lit? Can you see the rest of the Moon, glowing faintly?
flow.kid: Just after sunset, look west, low down, with a grown-up. Find a thin curved Moon. Draw it, with the buildings under it. Write the date and the time.
flow.parent: A thin crescent sets soon after the Sun, so look within an hour of sunset. In a city, buildings may hide it. Then look again the next evening, when it is higher. Try to look at the same time each evening. In India, the thin evening crescent often lies on its back, like a boat. The faint glow on the rest of the Moon is earthshine.
flow.context: This is the first night of the Moon diary. A Moon diary is a record of the Moon's shape, place and time, night after night, so you can find its pattern yourself.

flow.do: 1. Every second evening, go to the same spot at the same time. 2. Draw the Moon's shape. 3. Write the date, the time and the direction you faced. 4. Around the seventh night, look along the Moon's straight edge with binoculars, if you have them.
flow.wait: Come back every second evening, at the same time, until Purnima.
flow.say: Same place, same time. Has it grown? Has it moved? Which way are you facing to see it now?
flow.kid: Same time, same window. Draw the Moon again. Has it grown? Which way do you face?

ask.q: Each evening at the same time, where is the Moon compared with last time?
good: Further east, further from where the Sun set.
It started low in the west and moved round to the south.

flow.parent: Each evening at the same time, the growing Moon is further east, because it has moved along its orbit. For the first week it also climbs higher. The half Moon is high in the south at sunset. After that, the Moon is lower each evening, in the south-east and then the east. So you may need a different window as the days pass. Along the straight edge of a half Moon, binoculars show mountains and craters casting long shadows. On cloudy nights, just write 'cloudy'. Gaps are normal, and real scientists have them too.

flow.do: 1. On Purnima, go to an east-facing window or balcony at sunset. 2. Watch the full Moon rise above the buildings and note the time. 3. The next night, look at the same time. Is the Moon up yet?
flow.wait: Wait for Purnima, about two weeks after Amavasya.
flow.say: Tonight the Moon rises in the east as the Sun sets in the west. Tomorrow, will it be up at the same time?
flow.kid: Purnima! Face east at sunset. Watch the full Moon rise. Write the time. Tomorrow, go out at the same time. Is the Moon there yet?
flow.parent: The Moon rises on average about 50 minutes later each day. So the night after Purnima, it may not have risen yet at the same time. That is the start of the shrinking half of the month, Krishna Paksha. From now on, the Moon is up late at night and in the morning.

flow.do: 1. A few days after Purnima, look for the Moon in the western sky in the morning. Look before school or on the way. 2. Then lay all your drawings in a row, in date order, and talk about the pattern.
flow.say: Look at all your drawings in a row. What pattern do you see? Which side was lit while it was growing? Which side is lit now?
flow.kid: Look for the Moon in the morning sky, in the west. Then lay all your drawings in a row. What pattern can you see?

check.q: In your diary, which side of the Moon was lit while it was growing, in the evenings?
options: The right side, towards where the Sun set
The left side
It changed every night
check.why: The lit side always faces the Sun. In the evening the Sun has set in the west, to the right of the Moon when you face it. So a growing Moon is lit on its right. After Purnima, the lit side swaps to the left. Picking 'it changed every night' usually means some nights were missed or drawn from memory. Look again at your drawings.

flow.think: If you kept your diary for a whole year, how many Purnimas would you draw? Would it be exactly 12?

activities.context: This is a diary you keep for about two weeks. Every second evening, you draw the Moon's shape, write the time and the direction, and in the end you find its pattern for yourself.

activities.title: Sun or Moon? The Festival Calendar Hunt

materials.item: this year's wall calendar that marks Amavasya, Purnima and festivals, or one printed from the internet
12 slips of paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Find festivals on the calendar. Sort them into Moon festivals and Sun festivals. Compare with last year.

activities.record: Two lists: festivals set by the Moon, and festivals set by the Sun. Next to each Moon festival, write its tithi or phase.

flow.do: 1. Write one festival on each slip. Use these 12: Diwali, Holi, Raksha Bandhan, Guru Purnima, Buddha Purnima and Eid al-Fitr. Then Ganesh Chaturthi, Karva Chauth, Makar Sankranti, Pongal, Baisakhi and Christmas. 2. Find each one on the calendar together.
flow.say: Let's find our festivals on the calendar. Look at the little Moon pictures. Is there a full Moon, a new Moon or no Moon sign on that day?
flow.kid: Find each festival on the calendar. Look for a little Moon sign on its date. Is it a full Moon, a new Moon, or none?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Festival Calendar Hunt. You use a calendar to find out which festivals follow the Moon and which follow the Sun.

flow.do: 1. Sort the slips into two piles: set by the Moon, and set by the Sun. 2. Then look up the same festivals last year, on the internet or on an old calendar, and compare the dates.
flow.say: Which festivals moved to a different date from last year? Which stayed almost the same?
flow.kid: Make two piles: Moon festivals and Sun festivals. Did a festival move to a new date since last year? Then it probably follows the Moon.
flow.parent: Moon festivals: Diwali (Amavasya), Holi, Raksha Bandhan, Guru Purnima and Buddha Purnima (Purnima), Ganesh Chaturthi (the fourth tithi of the bright half), Karva Chauth (the fourth tithi of the dark half, ending at moonrise), Eid al-Fitr (when the new crescent is seen). Sun festivals: Makar Sankranti and Pongal (about 14 January), Baisakhi (about 13 or 14 April), and Christmas (25 December). Eid moves about 11 days earlier every year. The Hindu Moon festivals jump about, but stay in the same season, because of the extra month added every few years.

check.q: Makar Sankranti falls on about 14 January every year. Diwali's date changes. Why?
options: Makar Sankranti follows the Sun, and Diwali follows the Moon
Diwali follows the Sun, and Makar Sankranti follows the Moon
Someone chooses new dates each year
check.why: Makar Sankranti marks a point in the Sun's yearly path, so it stays on nearly the same date of our Sun calendar. Diwali falls on an Amavasya, a Moon day. Moon months are a little shorter than Sun months, so Moon festivals land on different dates each year. Picking 'someone chooses' is understandable. But nobody picks new dates each year. The dates follow the Sun or the Moon by fixed rules.

flow.do: Talk about why people long ago counted by the Moon.
flow.say: Before printed calendars, how could a whole village agree on the day of a festival?
flow.kid: Long ago there were no printed calendars. How could a whole village know when the festival was? Look up!
flow.think: Anyone, anywhere, can look up and see the Moon's shape. Is a calendar in the sky fairer than one printed on paper? Who decided our calendars?

activities.context: In this activity you use a calendar to sort festivals into ones set by the Moon and ones set by the Sun.

activities.title: Earthshine and the Daytime Moon

materials.item: a calendar that marks Amavasya and Purnima
binoculars, if you have them

activities.safety: In the daytime, never look at the Sun, and never point binoculars anywhere near it. Stand where a wall or tree blocks the Sun.

schedule.what: Two to four days after Amavasya, just after sunset, look at the crescent Moon for earthshine.
Two to five days after Purnima, look for the Moon in the morning sky in the west.

activities.record: Draw the crescent with the faint grey circle of earthshine. Draw the daytime Moon in the blue sky, with the time.

flow.do: 1. Two to four days after Amavasya, go to a west-facing window or balcony within an hour after sunset. 2. Find the thin crescent Moon low in the west. 3. Look carefully at the dark part. Use binoculars if you have them.
flow.say: Look at the dark part of the Moon. Can you see the whole round Moon, glowing very faintly? Where could that light be coming from?
flow.kid: Look at the dark part of the thin Moon. Can you see a faint grey circle? That light came from the Sun. It bounced off the Earth onto the Moon.
flow.parent: This faint glow is earthshine: sunlight bounced off the Earth, onto the Moon, and back to us. Leonardo da Vinci explained it about 500 years ago. It is easiest to see on a thin crescent, against a darkening sky. City lights and haze can hide it. Binoculars help a lot.
flow.context: This is the first step of Earthshine and the Daytime Moon. You look for the faint glow of earthshine on the dark part of a thin crescent Moon.

flow.do: 1. Two to five days after Purnima, go out in the morning, between sunrise and about 9 o'clock. 2. Stand where a wall or tree blocks the Sun. 3. Look in the western half of the sky for the pale Moon.
flow.wait: Wait until two to five days after Purnima.
flow.say: Is the Moon only a night thing? Let's look in the morning, opposite the Sun.
flow.kid: With a grown-up, look for the Moon in the morning sky. Look away from the Sun, to the west. Can you find it, pale and white?

check.q: Why can you see the Moon in the daytime?
options: The Moon is still above the horizon, and it is bright enough to see against the blue sky
There are two Moons, one for day and one for night
The Moon only shows in the daytime when it is cloudy
check.why: The Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day, so for half of the month it is up during some of the daytime. It is much brighter than any star, so it shows even against a blue sky. Picking 'two Moons' is a sweet idea, but there is only one Moon, and it is the same one you saw at night.

flow.think: When you see a thin crescent from Earth, someone on the Moon would see a big, nearly full Earth. What would the Earth look like from the Moon on Purnima?

activities.context: This activity has two short sky watches. First, you look for earthshine, the faint glow on the dark part of a crescent Moon. Then you find the Moon in the daytime sky.

activities.title: Act It Out: the Night the Moon Was Born

materials.item: a red or orange dupatta, a smaller ball and a bigger ball, or two cushions
some open space on a soft floor

activities.safety: Pretend to crash. Do not really bump into each other. Act on a mat or carpet.

schedule.what: Act out the giant crash, the ring of hot rock and the Moon gathering.

activities.record: Draw a comic strip in four boxes: the crash, the ring of rock, the Moon gathering, and the Moon today.

flow.do: Choose roles. One player is the young Earth, glowing hot. One is Theia, a planet the size of Mars. Others can be lumps of hot rock.
flow.say: About four and a half billion years ago, the Earth was young and hot. There was no Moon in its sky. Another planet, Theia, was on a crash course.
flow.kid: Choose who you are. Be the young Earth, the planet Theia, or hot rock. There is no Moon yet!
flow.context: This is the first step of the Moon's birth play. It acts out the main idea of how the Moon was made: a giant crash between the young Earth and another planet.

flow.do: 1. Theia moves slowly towards the Earth and pretends to hit it with a glancing blow, from the side, not head on. 2. The Earth spins round. 3. The rock players swirl round the Earth in a ring, holding the dupatta like a ring of hot rock. 4. Slowly, the rock players gather together into one Moon, and go round the Earth.
flow.say: Theia hits the Earth from the side. Hot rock splashes out and swirls round the Earth in a ring. Now, slowly, the lumps gather together. What have they made?
flow.kid: Theia, crash into the Earth from the side, gently! Rocks, swirl round the Earth in a ring. Now gather together into one Moon.
flow.parent: Scientists think the crash was a glancing blow, because only a blow from the side gives computer models a Moon like ours, and the Earth's fast spin. Some think the ring took years to gather. A newer idea, from computer models in 2022, is that the Moon may have formed in only a few hours.

flow.do: Talk about the clues that make scientists think this happened.
flow.say: Nobody saw this. So how do scientists know? Moon rocks are very like the Earth's outer rock. And the Moon has only a tiny iron middle. What would a crash that splashed out the Earth's outer rock do?
flow.kid: Nobody saw this happen! How do we know? Moon rocks are very like Earth rocks. Why might that be?

check.q: Which clue helps scientists think the Moon was made from splashed-out Earth rock?
options: Moon rocks are very like the rocks of the Earth's outer layers
The Moon is round
The Moon shines at night
check.why: Astronauts brought back Moon rocks, and scientists found they are almost a perfect match for the Earth's outer rock. A crash that splashed out the Earth's outer layers would make a Moon like that. Picking 'the Moon is round' is a fair guess, but all big moons and planets are round, because gravity pulls them into balls. That does not tell us how they were made.

flow.think: If the Moon was made partly from the Earth, is the Moon a piece of home?

activities.context: This is a short play about how the Moon was probably made: a planet called Theia crashing into the young Earth.

projects.title: A Moon Wheel: a paper calendar that shows tonight's Moon

materials.item: two paper plates or two circles of card, one a little smaller than the other
a split pin (a brass paper fastener), or a short pencil stub pushed through both
scissors, a pencil, a black crayon and a ruler
a calendar that marks Amavasya and Purnima

projects.safety: A grown-up cuts the window in the top plate and makes the hole in the middle.

schedule.what: Draw the 8 Moon shapes round the bottom plate. Cut a window in the top plate. Join the plates. Set it to tonight.
Turn the wheel on one step. Go outside and check the real Moon against the wheel.

projects.record: Write the dates of the next Amavasya and Purnima on your wheel. Write whether the wheel matched the real Moon.

flow.do: 1. With a ruler, draw lines across the bigger plate to divide it into 8 equal slices, like a pizza. 2. In each slice, halfway between the centre and the edge, draw one Moon shape, in this order. New, growing crescent, growing half, growing gibbous. Then full, shrinking gibbous, shrinking half, shrinking crescent. 3. Colour the dark parts black.
flow.say: We'll make a wheel that shows the Moon for any night. First, draw the 8 shapes in order round the plate.
flow.kid: Divide the big plate into 8 slices. In each slice, draw one Moon shape, in order round the plate. Colour the dark parts black.
flow.parent: Remember that a growing Moon seen from India is lit on the right, and a shrinking Moon on the left. Under each shape, write how many days after Amavasya it comes: 0, 4, 7, 11, 15, 18, 22, 26.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Moon Wheel project. You make a paper wheel that shows what shape the Moon will be on any night.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts a window in the smaller plate, halfway out from the centre. It must be big enough to show one Moon shape. 2. A grown-up makes a hole through the middle of both plates. 3. Put the smaller plate on top and join them with a split pin, so the top plate turns.
flow.say: Now let's join the plates, so the window can turn round to each Moon.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to cut a window in the small plate. They make a hole in the middle. Join the plates with a split pin. Turn the top plate. Does each Moon show in the window?

flow.do: 1. Find tonight's date on the calendar. 2. Count how many days it is since the last Amavasya. 3. Turn the window to the shape closest to that number. 4. Write the names Shukla Paksha on the growing half of the wheel and Krishna Paksha on the shrinking half.
flow.say: How many days since Amavasya? Turn the window to that shape. That's what the Moon should look like tonight.
flow.kid: Count the days since the last Amavasya. Turn the window to that Moon. Write 'Shukla Paksha' on the growing side and 'Krishna Paksha' on the shrinking side.

check.q: It is 7 days since Amavasya. Which shape should the wheel show?
options: A growing half Moon, lit on the right
A full Moon
A shrinking crescent
check.why: A full round of the Moon takes about 29 and a half days. A quarter of that is about 7 days. So a week after Amavasya, the Moon is a quarter of the way round, and we see a half Moon, lit on the right. Picking 'full Moon' usually means counting a week as half the month. The full Moon comes after about 15 days.

challenges.title: Keep Diwali in Autumn: design a Moon calendar
challenges.problem: Twelve Moon months add up to about 354 days. The Sun's year, which brings the seasons, is about 365 days. If a calendar only counts Moon months, its festivals drift about 11 days earlier every year. In about 16 years, Diwali would land in the hot months of April or May instead of autumn. Design a calendar rule that keeps the Moon months and stays in step with the seasons.
constraints: Every month must still begin on an Amavasya or a Purnima.
The rule must be simple enough for a village to follow without a computer.
Festivals must stay in the same season, year after year.
general: Add a whole extra Moon month about once every three years. Indian calendars do this. The extra month is called adhik maas.
Add 7 extra months in every 19 years. The Jewish calendar and the old Greek astronomer Meton used this rule.
Let the festivals drift through the seasons. The Islamic calendar does this, so Ramzan comes in every season over about 33 years.
creative: Watch for a natural sign each year, like the first new Moon after the mango trees flower, to decide when the year begins.
Watch the Sun as well as the Moon. If the Sun does not move into a new zodiac sign during a whole Moon month, make that month an extra one. Indian calendars use this rule to choose the adhik maas.
Make a calendar with two kinds of years, long and short, in a pattern you can remember.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own rule. Test it on paper for 10 years. Does your Diwali stay in autumn?

flow.do: 1. Work out together how many days 12 Moon months take: about 29 and a half days times 12. 2. Compare it with 365 days.
flow.say: One Moon month is about 29 and a half days. Twelve of them make about 354 days. The Sun's year is 365 days. How many days short are we?
flow.kid: Twelve Moon months make about 354 days. The Sun's year is 365 days. How many days short is that? Work it out.

options: 11 days
1 day
30 days
check.why: 365 minus 354 is 11. So a calendar of 12 Moon months falls 11 days behind the seasons every year. After 3 years it is 33 days behind, more than a whole Moon month. Picking 30 days usually means mixing up one month's length with the gap.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Keep Diwali in Autumn challenge. You find out why a calendar of Moon months slowly drifts away from the seasons.

flow.parent: After 3 years the drift is 33 days, more than one Moon month. So adding one extra month every three years or so brings the calendar back. That is the idea of adhik maas.

flow.do: 1. Invent a rule. 2. Test it in your table for 10 years. 3. See whether the drift stays small.

flow.think: The Islamic calendar lets Ramzan move through all the seasons. Some people like that, because everyone gets Ramzan in summer and in winter, in turn. Is drifting through the seasons a problem, or a kind of fairness?

challenges.title: Talk to the Far Side
challenges.problem: A rover has landed on the far side of the Moon. It cannot send messages straight to the Earth, because the whole Moon is in the way. Design a way to get a torch signal from 'the Earth' to a toy 'rover' hidden behind a big pot, which is the Moon.
constraints: The torch must stay at 'the Earth', on one side of the room.
You cannot move the pot or the rover.
The light must land on the rover, so it could read the message.
materials: a big pot, bucket or box as the Moon
a small toy as the rover
general: Put a mirror out beyond the Moon, where it can see both the Earth and the rover, to bounce the signal round. China did this in 2018 with a relay satellite called Queqiao, for the Chang'e 4 rover.
Use two mirrors, one after the other, to send the light round a corner.
creative: Put several relays in a ring round the Moon, so there is always one in the right place.
Send the signal in a code of long and short flashes, so the rover can 'read' it.
Ask: could the rover send a message back the same way?
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way. Draw it first, then try it. How many mirrors do you need?

flow.do: 1. Put the pot in the middle of the floor. 2. Hide the toy rover close behind it. 3. Stand at the other side of the room with the torch. Try to shine light on the rover.
flow.say: This pot is the Moon. Our rover is on the far side. Try to shine the torch on it from here. Can you?
flow.kid: The pot is the Moon. The toy rover is behind it, on the far side. Shine your torch at it from across the room. Can the light reach it?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Talk to the Far Side challenge. You try to send a light signal to a toy rover hidden behind a pot, like a rover on the far side of the Moon.

flow.do: Before trying anything, draw three ideas together.

flow.kid: Draw three ideas first. How could you get the light round the pot?

flow.do: 1. A helper holds a mirror out to one side, beyond the pot, where they can see both the torch and the rover. 2. Shine the torch at the mirror. 3. The helper tilts the mirror slowly until the light lands on the rover.
flow.say: The mirror is our relay. Tilt it slowly. Can you make the light land on the rover?
flow.kid: Ask a helper to hold a mirror out beyond the pot. Shine the torch at it. Tilt the mirror slowly until the light hits the rover.
flow.parent: Hold the mirror by its edges, and never shine the reflected light into anyone's eyes. It takes some patience to find the right tilt. That is just what engineers had to work out for the real relay satellite.

check.q: Why can't a rover on the far side of the Moon talk to the Earth directly?
options: The Moon itself is in the way
The far side is always dark
Radio does not work in space
check.why: The far side always faces away from the Earth, so the whole Moon blocks a straight line between them. A relay out beyond the Moon can see both. Picking 'always dark' is a common mix-up. The far side gets just as much sunlight as the near side. Radio works very well in space. That is how all spacecraft talk to us.

flow.think: The relay satellite Queqiao is named after a bridge of magpies in an old Chinese story, which lets two separated lovers meet once a year. Why do you think the engineers chose that name?

quiz.p: Why does the Moon seem to change shape during the month?
opts: We see more or less of its sunlit half as it goes round us
The Earth's shadow covers part of it
quiz.why: Half the Moon is always lit by the Sun. As it goes round us, we see different amounts of that half. Picking 'the Earth's shadow' is the most common wrong answer. The Earth's shadow only reaches the Moon in a lunar eclipse.

quiz.p: Remember the ball and lamp experiment. When the ball was between you and the lamp, what did you see?
opts: A dark ball: a new Moon
quiz.context: This question is about the ball and lamp experiment. A lamp is the Sun, a pale ball on a pencil is the Moon, and your head is the Earth. You turn slowly and watch the ball's lit part.
quiz.why: The lit side faced the lamp, away from you, so you saw a dark ball. That is the new Moon, Amavasya. Picking 'full Moon' usually means thinking the Moon is brightest when nearest the Sun.

quiz.p: Which comes straight after the full Moon?
quiz.why: After Purnima, the Moon shrinks a little at a time: gibbous, then half, then crescent, then new. Picking 'new Moon' skips the two weeks of shrinking in between.

quiz.p: In your Moon diary, you draw the Moon at the same time every second evening. What do you notice about where it is?
opts: It is further east each time
It is always in exactly the same place
quiz.context: A Moon diary is a record of the Moon's shape, the date, the time and the direction, kept night after night.
quiz.why: The growing Moon moves further round its orbit each day, so at the same time each evening it is further east, further from where the Sun set. Picking 'the same place' usually means only looking once or twice, or at different times.

quiz.p: The full Moon rises at about…
quiz.why: The full Moon is opposite the Sun, so it rises in the east as the Sun sets in the west. Picking 'midnight' is when the full Moon is highest, not when it rises.

quiz.p: Why do we always see the same face of the Moon?
opts: It spins once for each trip round the Earth
It does not spin at all
The far side is always dark
quiz.why: The Moon spins exactly once each trip round us, so its face stays towards us. Picking 'does not spin' is the most common idea. But walking round a chair while facing it shows you turn once.

quiz.p: What made the Moon's spin match its trip round the Earth?
opts: The Earth's pull acted like a brake on the Moon's spin
It has always been like that
quiz.why: Long ago the Moon spun faster. The Earth's pull on a slight bulge in the Moon's rock slowed it down until spin and trip matched. This is called tidal locking. Picking 'always been like that' is understandable, but the evidence says it changed.

quiz.p: A solar eclipse can only happen at…
quiz.why: In a solar eclipse the Moon passes between the Sun and the Earth. That is where it is at new Moon. Picking 'full Moon' mixes it up with a lunar eclipse.

quiz.p: Remember the shadow experiment. Why can everyone who can see the Moon watch a lunar eclipse?
opts: The Earth's big shadow covers the whole Moon
The Moon's shadow covers the whole Earth
quiz.context: This question is about the shadow experiment. A torch is the Sun, a football is the Earth and a lime is the Moon.
quiz.why: The football's shadow swallowed the whole lime. The Earth's shadow is big enough to cover the whole Moon, so anyone who can see the Moon sees it go dark. Picking 'the Moon's shadow covers the whole Earth' is backwards: the Moon's shadow is small.

quiz.p: Why isn't there a lunar eclipse every Purnima?
opts: The Moon's path is tilted, so it usually misses the Earth's shadow
Rahu only eats the Moon sometimes
The Earth has no shadow on some nights
quiz.why: The Moon's path is tilted a little, so most months it passes above or below the shadow. Picking 'Rahu' comes from an old story. Astronomers kept the name Rahu for one of the two crossing points of the paths.

quiz.p: How many tithis are there in one lunar month?
quiz.why: Each lunar month has 30 tithis, 15 in the bright half and 15 in the dark half. Picking 7 mixes it up with the days of a week.
Diwali falls on an Amavasya, so the sky is dark. Its date changes every year because it follows the Moon. Picking 'Purnima' mixes it up with festivals like Holi and Guru Purnima.

quiz.p: What do most scientists think made the Moon?
opts: A planet about the size of Mars crashed into the young Earth
The Earth caught a passing Moon
It has always been there, since the universe began
quiz.why: Moon rocks are very like the Earth's outer rock, and the Moon has a tiny iron centre. A giant crash explains both. Picking 'caught a passing Moon' was an old idea, but a captured Moon would probably be made of different rock.

quiz.p: What do scientists still argue about?
opts: Whether the Moon formed in years or in hours, from one crash or many
Whether the Moon goes round the Earth
quiz.why: The Moon going round us, and moonlight being sunlight, are settled. The details of the Moon's birth are still argued about, using computer models and rock clues.

quiz.p: Who wrote in 499 CE that eclipses are caused by shadows, not by a demon?
quiz.why: Aryabhata wrote it in the Aryabhatiya, in the part called the Golapada. Galileo and Newton lived more than 1,000 years later.

quiz.p: Wang Zhenyi explained lunar eclipses with a model. What did she use for the Earth?
quiz.why: The round table was the Earth, the lamp was the Sun and the mirror was the Moon. The table's round shadow fell on the mirror, as the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.

quiz.p: Which of these keeps time by the Moon?
opts: Corals that release their eggs together after a full Moon
quiz.why: Many corals spawn together on a few nights after a full Moon each year. Dung beetles also steer by moonlight. Pebbles and toys have no body clock that follows the Moon.

applications: Calendars in India and many other places count months by the Moon, and set festival dates by its tithis.
Fishing families and port officers use tide tables. The biggest tides, spring tides, come at new Moon and full Moon.
Astronomers predict eclipses to the minute, hundreds of years ahead, so scientists and families can travel to see them.
Eclipses let scientists study the Sun's faint outer glow, the corona, and once revealed a new element, helium.
Lasers bounced off mirrors on the Moon measure its distance to within a few millimetres, and test ideas about gravity.
Relay satellites, like China's Queqiao, let rovers on the far side of the Moon talk to the Earth.
Scientists study earthshine to measure how much sunlight the whole Earth reflects, which helps them study its clouds.
The way the Moon makes the Earth wobble is like the way planets make their stars wobble. Astronomers use those wobbles to find planets round other stars.
India's Chandrayaan missions study the Moon's south pole, where ice may one day give water to astronauts.
Night-time wildlife surveys plan around the Moon, because many animals behave differently on bright nights.

open_questions.q: Exactly how was the Moon made?
open_questions.why_open: Most scientists think a giant crash made it. But they argue about whether it was one crash or many, and whether the Moon formed in hours or over years. Computer models give different answers.

open_questions.q: Why are Moon rocks such a close match for the Earth's rocks?
open_questions.why_open: In many computer crashes, the Moon ends up made mostly of the other planet, Theia. Yet its rocks match the Earth's almost perfectly. Nobody has fully explained this.

open_questions.q: Why are the near side and the far side of the Moon so different?
open_questions.why_open: The near side has big dark lava seas, and the far side has almost none and a thicker crust. Scientists have several ideas, and rock from the far side, brought back in 2024, is being studied.

open_questions.q: Are the leftovers of Theia hidden deep inside the Earth?
open_questions.why_open: Two huge blobs of unusual rock sit deep in the Earth, near its core. Some scientists think they could be pieces of Theia. It is an idea still being tested.

open_questions.q: Why does the rising Moon look so much bigger?
open_questions.why_open: People have argued about the Moon illusion for more than 2,000 years. Ideas involve how the brain judges distance and size. Nobody has a full answer.

open_questions.q: Does the Moon affect how people sleep?
open_questions.why_open: A few studies found people sleep later and less before a full Moon. Others found no effect. More careful studies are needed.

open_questions.q: Would there be life on Earth without the Moon?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists think the Moon keeps the Earth's tilt steady, which keeps our seasons gentle. Others think the Earth would have stayed fairly steady anyway.

open_questions.q: How much water ice is hidden at the Moon's poles?
open_questions.why_open: Spacecraft, including India's Chandrayaan-1, found signs of water. How much ice there is in the dark craters, and how easy it is to reach, is not yet known.

maths.problem: Your Moon diary counts days from Amavasya, day 0. Purnima comes about 15 days later. If Amavasya is on 2 November, on about which date will Purnima be? Use a calendar to count.
maths.explain: Start at 2 November and count on 15 days: 3, 4, 5 and so on up to 17. So Purnima is about 17 November. The real date can be a day different, because tithis are not exactly one day long.
maths.context: A Moon diary is a record of the Moon's shape, the date, the time and the direction, kept night after night. It starts around Amavasya, the new Moon, and runs past Purnima, the full Moon.
maths.why_maths: Counting on a calendar lets you plan your Moon diary, so you know which night to go out and watch the full Moon rise.

maths.problem: The full Moon rose at 6:00 in the evening on Purnima. The Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day. At about what time will it rise 3 days later?
maths.explain: Each day adds about 50 minutes. Three days add 50 + 50 + 50 = 150 minutes. 150 minutes is 2 hours and 30 minutes, because 120 minutes make 2 hours. 6:00 plus 2 hours and 30 minutes is 8:30.
maths.context: In the Moon diary, you watch the full Moon rise on Purnima and notice it rises later each night after that.

answer_chart.title: Moonrise after Purnima, at about 50 minutes later each day

maths.why_maths: Adding times tells you when to go out to see the Moon, instead of waiting in the dark and guessing.

maths.problem: In the ball and lamp experiment, half the ball was lit. At half Moon, you could see half of that lit half. What fraction of the whole ball could you see lit?
maths.explain: The lamp lights half the ball. At half Moon, you see only half of that half. Half of a half is a quarter. The name 'quarter Moon' comes from something else: it comes a quarter of the way through the month. But this fraction is an easy way to remember the name.
maths.context: This question is about the ball and lamp experiment. A lamp is the Sun, a pale ball on a pencil is the Moon, and your head is the Earth. You turn slowly and watch the ball's lit part.
maths.why_maths: Fractions show exactly how much of the Moon we see lit at half Moon.

maths.problem: Look at this pattern of Moon shapes: new, crescent, half, gibbous, full, gibbous, half, crescent, new, crescent… What are the next three shapes?
maths.explain: The pattern repeats every 8 shapes: new, crescent, half, gibbous, full, gibbous, half, crescent. After 'new, crescent', it starts again, so the next shapes are half, gibbous, full.
maths.context: This question is about the ball and lamp experiment. A lamp is the Sun, a pale ball on a pencil is the Moon, and your head is the Earth. You turn slowly and watch the ball's lit part. Turning all the way round shows the Moon's shapes in a repeating order.
maths.why_maths: Seeing the Moon's shapes as a repeating pattern lets you predict the Moon for any night, like the people who made the first calendars.

maths.problem: Twelve Moon months are about 354 days. A Sun year is 365 days. How many days short is a Moon year? How many days short after 3 years?
maths.answer: 11 days in one year, and 33 days after 3 years.
maths.explain: 365 take away 354 is 11. So each Moon year is 11 days short. After 3 years: 11 + 11 + 11 = 33 days. That is more than one Moon month of about 29 and a half days. So adding one extra month about every 3 years brings the calendar back in step.
maths.context: In the Keep Diwali in Autumn challenge, you design a calendar that counts Moon months but stays in step with the seasons.

answer_chart.title: How far a 12-month Moon calendar falls behind the seasons

maths.why_maths: The subtraction shows why Indian calendars add an extra month, adhik maas, about once every three years.

maths.problem: In Eclipse Hunters, 2 of the 10 tilt cards say ON THE LINE. Each time your Moon passes full Moon, is an eclipse likely or unlikely?
maths.answer: Unlikely. Only 2 cards out of 10 give an eclipse, and 8 out of 10 do not.
maths.explain: There are 10 cards. 2 give an eclipse and 8 do not. 8 is much more than 2. So most times your Moon passes full Moon, there is no eclipse. The real sky is like this too.
maths.context: In the board game Eclipse Hunters, your Moon token goes round the Earth. Each time it passes new or full Moon you turn a tilt card to see whether there is an eclipse.
maths.why_maths: Thinking about likely and unlikely explains why eclipses are rare, even though there is a full Moon every month.

roots.context: We have been learning why the Moon changes shape, why it shows us one face, and how shadows make eclipses. Now we ask what the Moon's shapes tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the lamp test, the ball was always half lit, and only its place changed. From different places you saw a dark ball, a crescent, a half and a full circle. The real Moon is always half lit by the Sun too. So the shape we see each night shows where the Moon is, compared with the Sun and us.
deep_truth.habit: We say the Moon 'grows' and 'shrinks', and call it 'new' or 'full', as if the Moon itself changed. It never does. The names describe where the Moon is, compared with the Sun and with us.
deep_truth.evidence: In the lamp test, one ball that never changed gave every Moon shape, just because you turned on the spot. On any night, everyone on Earth sees the same phase, because the phase is set by where the Sun, the Earth and the Moon are.

three.who_am_i: A Moon phase is how the Moon looks from where you stand, on the Earth. Your place is part of every shape you see.
three.what_is_life: Corals time their egg-laying by the Moon, and dung beetles steer by moonlight. Life on Earth has grown up with the Moon's monthly rhythm.
three.what_is_this_world: The Moon is always half lit by the Sun. The shape we see changes with where the Moon is, compared with the Sun and the Earth.

roots.thread: Moonlight is sunlight that has bounced off the Moon. So every phase you see is made by the Sun, the Moon and the Earth together, at that moment. The Moon itself was probably made from the young Earth's rock, in a giant crash. The two still go round a shared point, and each has changed the other's spin. The Sun, the Earth and the Moon work as one system, and each Moon shape is one moment of it.

teachings.source: Isha Upanishad, opening verse (also Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 5.1.1)
teachings.teaching: That is whole, this is whole. From the whole, the whole comes out. Take the whole from the whole, and the whole remains.
teachings.link: Purnima comes from purna, whole. The Moon is whole on every night of the month, even on Amavasya. Only the part we see grows and shrinks.

teachings.teaching: Waking up is like the Moon reflected in water. The Moon does not get wet, and the water is not broken. The whole Moon, and the whole sky, shine even in one drop of dew.
teachings.link: One Moon shows in every puddle, pot of water and sea at the same time. In the same way, everyone on Earth sees the same Moon phase on the same night.

teachings.source: Jataka tale 316, the Sasa Jataka (the story of the hare)
teachings.teaching: A hare had nothing to give a hungry traveller, so it offered itself. To remember its kindness, the hare's shape was drawn on the Moon for everyone to see.
teachings.link: Many people in India and East Asia see a hare in the Moon's dark lava seas. We see the same hare every night because the Moon always shows us the same face.

science.text: The Earth and the Moon both go round a shared point inside the Earth. Each has changed the other: the Earth locked the Moon's spin, and the Moon slows the Earth's.
The Moon was probably made from the young Earth and another planet, mixed together in a giant crash. Exactly how is still being worked out.

other_view.view: The Moon is what it is by itself: a round ball of rock, half lit. Its phases are only how it looks to us. So they tell us about our place, and nothing about what the Moon really is.

practice.title: Find the Sun from the Moon
practice.say: If the Moon is up, let's look at it from the window. If not, look at a picture of it. Breathe in slowly while I count to four. Breathe out while I count to four. Now look at the lit side of the Moon and point the way it faces. The Sun is that way, even if it has set. Picture the Sun, the Moon and us, in a line or at an angle. Then think of everyone on Earth who sees this same shape tonight. Sit quietly together for one minute.
practice.kid: Look at the Moon, or a picture of it. Breathe in for four counts, out for four. Point the way the lit side faces. The Sun is that way. Who else sees this shape tonight?

ask: Everyone on Earth sees the same Moon phase tonight. Is the crescent in the Moon, or in the way we see it from here?
The Earth and the Moon were made from the same rock. Are they two things, or one?
Does the Moon matter only because we look at it, or for itself?

how_we_found_out.story: Long ago, many people thought the Moon made its own light. Old stories said it really wasted away and grew back each month. In India, a story said an eclipse happened when the demon Rahu swallowed the Sun or the Moon. Careful sky-watchers noticed something those ideas could not explain. The bright side of the Moon always points towards the Sun. A thin crescent is always close to the Sun in the sky, and a full Moon is always opposite it. About 2,450 years ago in Greece, Anaxagoras said the Moon shines with the Sun's light. In 499 CE, the Indian astronomer Aryabhata wrote in the Aryabhatiya that the half of the Moon facing the Sun is bright, and the other half is dark. He wrote that in a solar eclipse the Moon covers the Sun, and in a lunar eclipse the Earth's shadow covers the Moon. With this idea, astronomers could work out the day and time of an eclipse long before it came. A demon could not be predicted, but shadows could be calculated. Indian astronomers kept the names Rahu and Ketu, but used them for the two points in the sky where eclipses can happen.
how_we_found_out.who: Anaxagoras (Greece, about 450 BCE) and Aryabhata (India, 499 CE)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: The Moon makes its own light and really grows and shrinks, and a demon swallows it in an eclipse. The lit side always facing the Sun, and eclipses worked out in advance from shadows, showed these ideas were wrong.
